title: You Will Receive Power
subtitle: Acts 1:1–11
description: Luke opens his second volume where his Gospel ended: forty days of the risen Jesus, one command to wait, and a promise that maps the whole book.
paragraphs: The second volume opens with a letter's greeting and a claim about the first: “In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach.” Began. Luke's Gospel, in its author's own reckoning, was only the start of what Jesus did, and this book is the continuation, written by the same hand to the same reader. The first book ran until the day he was taken up to heaven, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. What stands between the cross and that taking up is forty days of evidence: after his suffering, Jesus presented himself to them with many convincing proofs that he was alive. He appeared to them over a span of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. The risen Jesus of Acts does not drift off like a vision. He eats, he teaches, he builds a case, and the subject of the whole forty days is the kingdom.

And while they were gathered together, he gave them the order the whole book hangs on: wait. “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss.” The gift has a name they already know from his teaching, and a comparison attached to it: “For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” John's water went over a person. This baptism, a few days out, would come upon them, and the book's first word to its witnesses is not go but wait, in the city where their Lord was crucified weeks before, among the people who crucified him. Everything in Acts waits on this gift arriving, and Luke is careful to put the waiting first.

The apostles heard kingdom and reached for the map they knew. So when they came together, they asked him, “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” It is the last question they ask him on earth, and it is the old hope in its national shape: the throne of David, the Romans gone, Israel restored. Jesus did not correct the hope. He took the timetable out of their hands: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority.” The kingdom would come on the Father's clock, not theirs, and the men who would carry it were not given the schedule. They were given something else instead, in the next breath, and it has organized every reading of this book since.

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” Power, not information. Witnesses, not rulers. And the mission is given as a geography: Jerusalem, where they are standing and where he was killed; all Judea and Samaria, the home country and the despised half of it; and the ends of the earth, which in their world had a capital called Rome. The book of Acts is this sentence unfolding, chapter by chapter, city by city, and it ends with the witnesses still on the road the sentence laid out, in the empire's heart, under guard, preaching. Everything between is the sentence keeping its word.

After he had said this, they watched as he was taken up, and a cloud hid him from their sight. No chariot, no whirlwind; a cloud received him the way clouds in Israel's story carry the presence of God, and the eyewitnesses stood looking intently into an empty sky. They were still looking when two men dressed in white stood beside them, heaven's witnesses answering earth's witnesses. “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.” The rebuke is gentle and the promise is exact: same Jesus, same way, back. The apostles' work was not sky-watching, and the book now turns them around, toward Jerusalem, toward the waiting, toward the gift a few days out.

title: The Twelfth Apostle
subtitle: Acts 1:12–26
description: The praying church fills Judas's empty place by lot, restoring the twelve witnesses before the Spirit comes.
paragraphs: They returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day's journey from the city, eleven men walking back down the road they had climbed that morning with twelve months of questions still unanswered and one sentence of promise to carry: wait. When they arrived, they went to the upper room where they were staying, and Luke lists them by name, the whole remaining college of the apostles: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. With one accord they all continued in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers. The brothers who had not believed in him during his life (John tells that plainly) are in the prayer room now. The first church in Acts is a praying room of about a hundred and twenty people, and its first business is not strategy. It is prayer, and then it is a vacancy.

In those days Peter stood up among the brothers and named the vacancy himself. “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus. He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” Judas had been one of the Twelve, a sharer in the same work, and his end is told in Luke's parenthesis with a frankness that does not flinch: with the reward for his wickedness Judas bought a field, and there he fell headlong and burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out. It became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so they called that field in their own language Akeldama, Field of Blood. Matthew's account of Judas's death differs in its details, and Luke leaves his version standing here without reconciling the two, the way this series leaves every seam Luke leaves.

Peter's argument runs on Scripture, as everything in this book will. “For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,’ and, ‘May another take his position.’” Two psalms, one for the empty place and one for the filled one. The office itself sets the qualification, and Peter states it like a job description written by the story so far: “Therefore it is necessary to choose one of the men who have accompanied us the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us. For one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection.” The replacement must be an eyewitness of the whole course, baptism to ascension, because the office is witness before it is anything else. Two men met the standard out of the hundred and twenty: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias.

And they prayed, in words Luke preserves because they show how the early church made a decision it refused to make alone: “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen to take up this ministry and apostleship, which Judas abandoned to go to his rightful place.” Then they cast lots, the old Israel way of asking heaven to choose, and the lot fell to Matthias, and he was added to the eleven apostles. Nothing more is ever said of Matthias in the New Testament, and Joseph Barsabbas disappears with the greater honor of having almost been chosen. The lots are the last of their kind in the Bible; after the Spirit comes, the church will decide differently. But the number is restored before Pentecost, twelve again, a full college of witnesses, because the promise is coming to a people made ready, and the first thing the Spirit will find is a vacancy already filled by prayer.

title: Tongues of Fire
subtitle: Acts 2:1–13
description: On Pentecost the Spirit fills the house with wind and fire, and Galileans declare God's wonders in the languages of the world.
paragraphs: When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place. Pentecost was Israel's feast of harvest firstfruits, fifty days after Passover, and Jerusalem was full of pilgrims for it. The hundred and twenty were still in one place, still waiting, on the morning the few days of Jesus' promise ran out. Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting. Luke reaches for comparisons because the event outruns description: a sound like wind, and then what they saw, tongues like flames of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them. On each of them, not on the Twelve only. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them. The baptism Jesus promised had arrived, and its first evidence was speech.

The sound did the gathering. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven, and when this sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard them speaking his own language. Astounded and amazed, they asked the question the whole chapter turns on: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language?” These are not ecstatic syllables needing interpretation in Luke's telling. They are the languages of the world the pilgrims came from, heard clearly by the people who spoke them at home, and Luke slows down to read the atlas aloud: Parthians, Medes, and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome, both Jews and converts to Judaism; Cretans and Arabs. East to west, the list runs like the table of nations read backward into one Jerusalem street.

And what the crowd heard in all those languages was not small talk: “we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!” The wonders of God, preached at nine in the morning by Galilean fishermen in the mother tongues of the whole known world. Luke, who organized his Gospel around a journey to Jerusalem, opens his second book with Jerusalem made briefly into the whole earth: the mission sentence of chapter 1, Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, gets its preview here, with the ends of the earth standing in the street listening. Astounded and perplexed, they asked one another, “What does this mean?” It is the right question, and this book will spend twenty-eight chapters answering it.

But not everyone asked it. Others mocked them and said, “They are drunk on new wine!” The two responses to Pentecost stand side by side in the street and they have stood side by side ever since: perplexity that asks what this means, and mockery that explains it away before it costs anything to look closer. Wine at the third hour of the day is a drunkard's charge, and it is the one Peter will pick up first when he stands to preach, because it lets him start where the crowd already is. The mockery, in Luke's economy, is not a failure of the morning. It is the sermon's opening.

title: This Is What Was Spoken
subtitle: Acts 2:14–41
description: Peter's first sermon runs from Joel's prophecy to the empty tomb, and three thousand are baptized before the day ends.
paragraphs: Then Peter stood up with the Eleven, lifted up his voice, and addressed the crowd. The man who denied Jesus three times in a courtyard seven weeks earlier now stands with the other eleven ranged around him and preaches to the city that crucified him, and he begins with the drunk charge. “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen carefully to my words. These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It is only the third hour of the day!” Nine in the morning. No serious drinker, and no feast day in Israel, starts there. The defense takes ten seconds, because Peter is not really defending. He is explaining: “No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.”

And he reads Joel's last-days oracle over a street full of fishermen speaking languages: “In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. Even on My menservants and maidservants I will pour out My Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.” Sons and daughters, young and old, servants and maidservants: the Spirit Joel promised does not respect the usual ranks, and the crowd in the street, slaves' tongues and women's voices among the speakers, is the exhibit. Peter reads the oracle to its end, into the darkened sun and the moon of blood and the great and glorious Day of the Lord, and lands on the sentence the whole sermon is aimed at: “And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Then the sermon turns from prophecy to a name. “Men of Israel, listen to this message: Jesus of Nazareth was a man certified by God to you by miracles, wonders, and signs, which God did among you through Him, as you yourselves know.” The life first, publicly certified, as you yourselves know. Then the death, with both hands of it named: “He was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross.” God's set plan and Jerusalem's guilt in one sentence, neither softened. And then the sermon's hinge: “But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip.” Impossible, Peter says, and he argues the impossibility out of David's psalm: “I saw the Lord always before me; because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope, because You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.”

The argument is a tomb they can walk to. “Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.” David's body decayed in a known grave, so David the prophet was speaking of his descendant: “God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses. Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.” And from David's other psalm comes the sermon's last text: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’” Then Peter closes the case in one sentence addressed to the whole nation: “Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!”

When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” It is the question the whole sermon was fishing for, and Peter's answer is the church's front door: “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off,” he said, “to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.” With many other words he testified and urged them, all morning, “Be saved from this corrupt generation.” Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day. The book's first count is a harvest number: the hundred and twenty became three thousand before the feast day ended.

title: They Devoted Themselves
subtitle: Acts 2:42–47
description: Luke's first summary of the church's life: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer, with the Lord adding daily.
paragraphs: Luke now does what he will do at every turning of this book: he stops the story and describes the life of the community the Spirit has made, in a summary meant to be read slowly. They devoted themselves, he says, and the verb is a staying verb, they kept on devoting themselves, to four things: the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Teaching first, doctrine from the men who had walked the whole course from John's baptism to the ascension. Fellowship, a shared life with shared goods, not an audience. The breaking of bread, the table they shared in houses where the Lord's death was remembered inside an ordinary meal. And prayer, the upper room habit carried out into the city. Everything Acts will narrate grows out of these four devotions or measures itself against them.

A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs. The awe and the wonders belong together in Luke's sentence: the signs did not merely amaze, they solemnized. All the believers were together and had everything in common. Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need. This was not a law laid on converts, and later chapters will show believers still owning the houses they meet in. It was what devotion looked like in a community where need was treated as a claim: property became a fund for whoever lacked, held loosely because the fellowship was held tightly.

With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart, praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. Public and private at once: daily in the great courts where any Jerusalemite could watch, and nightly at tables in homes across the city. Gladness and sincerity are Luke's chosen adjectives for the table, joy without performance. And the summary ends with the book's refrain in its first form, a sentence that gives the growth to its true author: and the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved. Not the apostles added, not the church added. The Lord added, daily, while the community did the four ordinary things it had devoted itself to. Luke will return to sentences like this one at every stage of the journey, as if to keep the bookkeeping straight about whose work the book of Acts is.

title: In the Name of Jesus
subtitle: Acts 3:1–10
description: Peter and John have no silver or gold, but a man lame from birth walks into the temple in the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
paragraphs: One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour, three o'clock, when the evening sacrifice drew the city uphill. And a man who was lame from birth was being carried the other way through his own daily routine: to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those entering the temple courts. Every day. Carried in, set down, carried home, for a lifetime of days, a fixture of the gate like the bronze itself. When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. It was the only sentence his life at the gate had ever required of him.

Peter looked directly at him, as did John, and told him to look at them. So the man gave them his attention, expecting to receive something from them, a coin assessed by eye the way he had assessed ten thousand worshipers. But Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” What I have: not a treasury, a name. Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once the man's feet and ankles were made strong. Feet and ankles, the parts that had never borne him, engineered in a moment. The gift was not handed over and hoped about. It was verified in the man's own joints before his eyes finished widening.

He sprang to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God. Walking and leaping: the careful steps of a beginner and the abandon of a worshiper in the same body in the same minute, through the gate he had only ever sat outside of, into courts he had only ever begged at the edge of. When all the people saw him walking and praising God, they recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. Recognition is the miracle's certificate in Luke's telling: not a stranger healed, but the gate's own beggar, the one everybody knew, on his feet inside.

The apostles had no silver and no gold, and Luke makes no apology for it. The church of Acts is poor in coin and rich in exactly one asset, the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and this episode is the name's first public expenditure since Pentecost. A man carried daily for more than forty years (the council hearing will supply his age) walks into the temple under his own power, and the wonder it makes is about to hand Peter a congregation larger than the one at Pentecost, gathered in Solomon's Colonnade, staring. The sermon is next, and characteristically, it will begin by giving the credit away.

title: The God of Abraham Has Glorified His Servant
subtitle: Acts 3:11–26
description: Over the healed beggar, Peter preaches the Author of life to the crowd in Solomon's Colonnade and calls them to repent.
paragraphs: While the man clung to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and ran to them in the walkway called Solomon's Colonnade, the covered porch on the temple's east side where Jesus himself had walked and taught in winter. The healed beggar clinging to the apostles made a picture no crier could have improved on, and Peter saw the crowd and did with it what he did at Pentecost: he preached, and his first move was to refuse the credit standing right in front of them. “Men of Israel, why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?”

“The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His servant Jesus. You handed Him over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though he had decided to release Him.” The titles pile up as the sermon goes, each one heavier than the last: the Holy and Righteous One, rejected while a murderer was asked for and released; and then the sermon's most staggering sentence, an accusation and a gospel in a single breath: “You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of this fact.” The Author of life, killed by his readers. And the man at their side is the paragraph's proof, and Peter explains him too: “By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence.” Name and faith, faith and name, the whole mechanism stated without a syllable about Peter's power or Peter's godliness.

Then the sermon does what Peter's preaching characteristically does at its sharpest point: it offers mercy to the people it has just convicted. “And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders. But in this way God has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer.” Their crime was prophecy's fulfillment, and their ignorance is read as the door of repentance rather than its barrier. “Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away,” he said, and beyond the wiping he holds out times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord and the sending of Jesus again, the Christ appointed for them, whom heaven must receive until the time comes for the restoration of all things. No preacher in the temple courts had ever been allowed to finish such a sermon, and it is a measure of the crowd's attention, and the beggar standing healed beside him, that Peter finishes his.

He closes where Moses began, with the prophet Moses promised: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you. Everyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people.” And he ends the sermon on the covenant's first family and the sermon audience's own first place in line: “Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.” “When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways.” First to you. The sermon that began with a lame man's ankles ends with an order of blessing that starts in this colonnade, and the temple authorities are already on their way through the crowd to stop it, which is how Luke tells you it was working.

title: No Other Name
subtitle: Acts 4:1–22
description: Before the Sanhedrin, Peter names Jesus the cornerstone and declares there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.
paragraphs: While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them, greatly disturbed, and the disturbance had a doctrine in it: they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead, and resurrection was the Sadducees' denied article. They seized Peter and John, and because it was evening, they put them in custody until the next day. The church's first night in jail is recorded without a tremor, and Luke slips the growth past the arrest in the next breath: but many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand. The sermon the authorities interrupted finished its work in custody.

The next day the rulers, elders, and scribes assembled in Jerusalem, the full Sanhedrin, along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and many others from the high priest's family, the same house that had tried Jesus weeks earlier. They had Peter and John brought in and began to question them with the right legal question: “By what power or what name did you do this?” Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, and Luke marks the filling because this is what the promised power looks like when it testifies: not tongues this time, but a defendant answering judges. “If we are being examined today about a kind service to a man who was lame, to determine how he was healed, then let this be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed.”

He reads their own psalm into the record: “This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’” And then Peter delivers, to the highest court of his nation, the sentence this whole series has been driving toward since the angel's first announcement: “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.” No other name, under heaven, given to men. When they saw the boldness of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they marveled and took note that these men had been with Jesus. The court's own minutes, as Luke reports them, record the transformation and its cause correctly. And seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response. The evidence stood in the room on its own two feet, over forty years old and formerly lame from birth, and there was no cross-examination for him.

So they ordered them to leave the Sanhedrin and conferred together, and Luke lets the reader hear the conference, which is the most honest minute the council keeps in the book: “What shall we do with these men?” they asked. “It is clear to everyone living in Jerusalem that a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it. But to keep this message from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.” Not refute. Not deny. Contain. Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John replied with the church's constitution in two sentences: “Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” Cannot stop: not will not, as a policy, but cannot, as a fact about witnesses. After further threats they let them go, because all the people were glorifying God for what had happened. The first trial of the church ends with the defendants released, the evidence walking home beside them, and the court's whole achievement a threat.

title: The Place Was Shaken
subtitle: Acts 4:23–37
description: The threatened church prays for boldness instead of safety, the place shakes, and Barnabas lays a field's price at the apostles' feet.
paragraphs: On their release, Peter and John returned to their own people and reported everything that the chief priests and elders had said to them. The report is the episode's quiet hinge: the church hears the threat from the men who received it, firsthand, and its response is not a strategy meeting. When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord, and Luke preserves the prayer because it is the community's theology stated under pressure. “Sovereign Lord,” they said, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. You spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David: ‘Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His Anointed One.’” A threatened church prays a psalm about raging rulers back to the God who wrote it, and finds its own morning already in the text.

Then the prayer does its boldest work: it names the conspiracy as fulfillment. Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel in this very city against God's holy servant Jesus, whom he anointed, and they carried out what God's hand and will had decided beforehand would happen. The cross itself, read this way, is not the conspiracy succeeding. It is God's plan being executed by the conspirators' own hands. And out of that reading comes the request, and the request is the surprise of the chapter. The church under threat does not ask for the threats to stop, or for safety, or for the rulers to be removed. “And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness, as You stretch out Your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.” Consider their threats, and give us more of what provoked them. After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly. The shaking is heaven's amen: the request granted in the room where it was made, Pentecost repeated as an answer to prayer rather than a date on a calendar.

Luke follows the prayer with the book's second great summary, money and all. The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned. With great power the apostles continued to give their testimony about the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and abundant grace was upon them all. There were no needy ones among them, because those who owned lands or houses would sell their property, bring the proceeds from the sales, and lay them at the apostles' feet for distribution to anyone as he had need. The phrase is chosen with care: at the apostles' feet, the proceeds surrendered to the community's judgment rather than distributed as private charity with the giver's name on it.

And then Luke gives the practice a face, deliberately, before he gives it its shadow. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas, meaning Son of Encouragement, sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet. It is the first thing this book ever tells us about Barnabas, who will carry its second half: not a sermon, not a miracle, a field converted quietly into the community's purse. Luke sets the example down last in the chapter so that the next chapter's counterfeit can be measured against it. The generosity is real, the grace is abundant, and the church is about to learn that even this can be faked, and what the Holy Spirit does about a lie told in a room full of grace.

title: You Have Lied to the Holy Spirit
subtitle: Acts 5:1–11
description: Ananias and Sapphira stage a generosity they did not practice, and the young church learns that the Spirit in the room is not safe to counterfeit.
paragraphs: Now a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, also sold a piece of property. Also: Luke's little word puts their sale in Barnabas's row, a field converted to cash like the Levite's field, and laid at the apostles' feet like his. But the likeness was staged. With his wife's full knowledge, he kept back some of the proceeds for himself, but brought a portion and laid it at the apostles' feet. The sin was not the keeping. Peter will say so himself: the land was his, and the money after the sale was at his disposal. The sin was the portion presented as the whole, generosity performed at a discount, a reputation for Barnabas-level surrender purchased with part of the price and all of the appearance.

Then Peter said, and the knowing in the question is the Spirit's own work in the room: “Ananias, how is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and withhold some of the proceeds from the land? Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? How could you conceive such a deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God!” Not lied to men, but to God: the court's verdict upgrades the fraud's victim. The apostles were not the deceived party in heaven's accounting. The Holy Spirit, present in the community the way fire was present in the tabernacle, was. On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. No sentence is pronounced, no hand is raised; exposure itself is the execution. And great fear came over all who heard what had happened. Then the young men stepped forward, wrapped up his body, and carried him out and buried him, and the church went on with its morning.

About three hours later his wife also came in, unaware of what had happened, and Peter gave her the one question that could have saved her if she had answered it with the truth: “Tell me,” said Peter, “is this the price you and your husband got for the land?” “Yes,” she answered, “that is the price.” The lie was maintained with the body of its co-author three hours buried, and Peter's answer closes the episode like a door: “How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?” Peter replied. “Look, the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.” At that instant she fell down at his feet and died, and the young men carried her out and buried her beside her husband.

And great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about these events. It is the first time in the New Testament that the word church is used of this community, and it arrives in a sentence about fear. Luke does not soften the story, defend it, or explain it away, and this series does not either: a married couple conspired to fake a devotion, the lie was exposed by the Spirit through Peter, and both died on the day of their offering, and the church that had prayed for boldness learned that the presence it carried was not safe to counterfeit. The fear is not the opposite of the grace of chapter 4. In Luke's telling, it is the grace's atmosphere, the weather of a community where God is actually in the room. What the fear produced comes next, and it is not retreat. It is a crowd in Solomon's Colonnade and sick people laid in the streets to catch an apostle's shadow.

title: We Must Obey God
subtitle: Acts 5:12–42
description: An angel redeploys the jailed apostles to the temple courts, Gamaliel counsels the council to wait, and the flogged men leave rejoicing.
paragraphs: The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and with one accord the believers gathered together in Solomon's Colonnade, the same porch where Peter had preached over the healed beggar. Although the people regarded them highly, no one else dared to join them, and yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord, large numbers of both men and women. Fear and growth in the same paragraph, awe keeping the casual away and conviction drawing the convinced in. As a result, people brought the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, so that at least Peter's shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by. Luke reports the hope without endorsing its mechanics, the way he reports everything the crowd believed, and crowds also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.

Then the high priest and all his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy, and arrested the apostles, all of them this time, and put them in the public jail. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out, saying, in the only voice in this episode that gives the apostles an order they will enjoy obeying: “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” At daybreak the apostles entered the temple courts as they had been told and began to teach the people. The jailbreak was not an escape. It was a redeployment, back to the exact courts they had been seized in, at the exact hour the court itself was assembling to try them.

When the high priest and his associates arrived, they convened the Sanhedrin, the full assembly of the elders of Israel, and sent to the jail for the apostles. But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there, and their report is the court's slow dawning in one sentence: “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” Then someone came in and announced the morning's whole absurdity: “Look, the men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people!” The captain went with the officers and brought the apostles, but not by force, for fear the people would stone them, the arresting party now afraid of the crowd the prisoners drew. Brought in and made to stand before the Sanhedrin, they heard the high priest's charge: “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.”

But Peter and the other apostles replied, and their five sentences are the sermon's shortest form: “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree. God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel. We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.” When the council members heard this, they were enraged, and they resolved to put the apostles to death. The trial was over; the execution was being scheduled, when a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law honored by all the people, stood up and ordered the men put outside for a short time. His argument was history, and it was cool where the room was hot: Theudas rose up with four hundred men and came to nothing; Judas the Galilean drew away people and perished and his followers scattered. “So in the present case I advise you: Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”

At this, they yielded to Gamaliel. They called the apostles in and had them flogged, the compromise between death and dignity, then ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them. The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. Rejoicing, with the flogging fresh. It is the first suffering in the book that lands on the witnesses' bodies, and its recorded effect is joy, a beatitude acted out within sight of the court that inflicted it. Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ. The court's order is on the record. So is the church's daily disobedience to it, in the same courts, in the same name.

title: The Seven Chosen
subtitle: Acts 6:1–7
description: A complaint about the widows' food line produces the Seven, all Greek names, chosen by the church and ordained with prayer.
paragraphs: In those days when the disciples were increasing in number, the Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. It is the church's first internal problem, and Luke states its anatomy exactly: growth, and two cultures inside one community, Greek-speaking Jews from the dispersion and Hebrew-speaking Jews from the homeland, and a daily mercy, the feeding of widows, where the Greek widows were being missed. Not persecuted. Overlooked, which is the quieter failure, the kind that grows inside a distribution system too big for its administrators. The church of Acts will face councils, mobs, and prisons; its first crisis is a food line.

So the Twelve summoned all the disciples and said, and their sentence draws the line that organizes the church's work from this day forward: “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables. Therefore, brothers, select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will assign this responsibility to them and will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” Not that tables are beneath apostles; that the word and prayer would be neglected for them is unacceptable. The community, not the apostles, does the selecting, and the qualification named for the food ministry is not accounting. It is men full of the Spirit and wisdom, because in this church there is no secular work, only work done by spiritual people or neglected by distracted ones.

This proposal pleased the whole group. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, as well as Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism. Read the names again: every one of the seven is Greek. The community answered a Greek complaint by handing the whole distribution to Greek men, the overlooked party given the trust instead of an apology. Luke lists all seven and then follows exactly two of them for the rest of the story, Stephen and Philip, which is his way of telling you the food line was a doorway. They presented these seven to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. Hands laid on, in prayer, for the waiting on tables: the church ordains its waiters with the same solemnity it will use for its missionaries.

So the word of God continued to spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem grew rapidly, and a great number of priests became obedient to the faith. This is Luke's third great summary, and its last clause is the stunner: priests, the temple's own caste, the colleagues of the men arresting the apostles, coming over in numbers. The crisis of the food line was settled with a structure and a prayer, and the settlement's fruit was not a quieter church but a faster-growing one. The book will now prove its own arrangement inspired: the first of the seven chosen to feed widows is about to become the church's first preacher to die for the word, and the second will carry the gospel out of Jerusalem entirely. The tables were never the lesser assignment. They were the seminary.

title: Stephen's Defense
subtitle: Acts 6:8–7:36
description: Arrested on arranged charges, Stephen answers with Israel's whole history: Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, the rejected deliverer sent back as redeemer.
paragraphs: Now Stephen, who was full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people. The first of the seven table-servers is on the street doing what the apostles do, and it draws the same fire. Resistance arose from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, diaspora Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and Asia, and they disputed with Stephen, but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke. So the argument was replaced by an arrangement: they prompted some men to say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God.” They stirred up the people, elders, and scribes, seized him, and brought him before the Sanhedrin, where false witnesses performed the charge in its polished form: “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. For we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.” And all who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel. Then the high priest asked Stephen, “Are these charges true?” What follows is not a plea. It is the longest speech in Acts, a retelling of Israel's whole history from the dock, and its answer to the charge is hidden in its pattern.

“Brothers and fathers, listen to me! The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and told him, ‘Leave your country and your kindred and go to the land I will show you.’” Stephen starts where the nation's faith starts, with a God who appears in Mesopotamia, outside the land, before there was a temple or a law. Abraham obeyed and inherited nothing, not even a foot of ground, only a promise and a prophecy of slavery: his descendants would be foreigners in a strange land, enslaved and mistreated four hundred years. “But I will punish the nation that enslaves them,” God said, “and afterward they will come forth and worship Me in this place.” God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and the line ran on, Abraham to Isaac to Jacob to the twelve patriarchs.

Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt, but God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles, and granted him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, until the rejected brother stood as ruler over Egypt and fed the very family that had sold him when famine swept Egypt and Canaan. Jacob came down with seventy-five souls and died in Egypt, and his bones were carried back to Shechem. Notice Stephen's rhythm, because the whole speech beats with it: the chosen one is rejected by his own brothers first, and exalted by God after. It happened to Joseph. Stephen is about to show it happened to Moses too, and the council will eventually hear where the pattern is aimed.

As the time drew near for God to fulfill his promise, another king arose over Egypt who knew nothing of Joseph, and Moses was born, beautiful in the sight of God, hidden three months, raised in Pharaoh's house, educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and powerful in speech and action. At forty years old Moses went out to his brothers and avenged a mistreated Israelite by striking down the Egyptian, assuming his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them. They did not. The next day, breaking up a fight between two Israelites, he was pushed aside with the question that Stephen quotes like a refrain: “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses fled to Midian and lived forty years as a foreigner, and the deliverer rejected at forty was still God's choice at eighty, when the angel appeared in the flames of a burning bush in the desert near Mount Sinai. “I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. I have indeed seen the oppression of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt.”

Stephen now gathers the whole Moses story into the sentence the speech was built to carry: “This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush. He led them out and performed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and for forty years in the wilderness.” The rejected one is the sent one; the question thrown in his face becomes his title. The defense rests its first half there, on history every man in the room confesses. What the fathers did with the deliverer after the Exodus is the second half, and it is not history anymore. It is an indictment, and Stephen is about to stop being careful.

title: Lord, Do Not Hold This Sin Against Them
subtitle: Acts 7:37–60
description: The defense becomes an indictment, Stephen sees the Son of Man standing, and the first martyr dies praying for his executioners while Saul watches.
paragraphs: The defense resumes with the promise Stephen's hearers cannot argue with, spoken by the deliverer they have just been reminded they rejected: Moses told the Israelites, “God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.” Moses was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with the fathers, and he received living words to pass on to them. Then Stephen's tense changes, and four hundred years collapse into the present tense of accusation: “But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. They said to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us! As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’” At that time they made a calf and offered sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their own hands. And God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, exactly as Amos had written: “Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? You have taken along the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.”

From the wilderness Stephen moves to the charge's other half, the holy place itself. The fathers carried the tabernacle of the Testimony through the wilderness, built exactly as God directed Moses, and brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations. It remained until David, who found favor with God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built the house for him. However, and with this word the defense turns its last corner, “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says: ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be? Has not My hand made all these things?’” The temple is real, and Solomon built it, and God never lived in it the way the charge supposes. Stephen has answered both counts out of Israel's own Scriptures: Moses was honored by being obeyed, and the temple is honored by remembering what it is not.

Then the defense stops being a defense. “You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did. Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. And now you are His betrayers and murderers,” he said, “you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it.” On hearing this, the members of the Sanhedrin were enraged, and they gnashed their teeth at him. The pattern of the whole speech had landed where it was aimed from the first sentence: Joseph's brothers, Moses' rejecters, the prophets' killers, and now this council, one long family habit of refusing the one God sends. No verdict is recorded. The speech itself was the verdict, and the court answers it the way the pattern predicts.

But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and he told them to look: he saw heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Standing, the only place in the New Testament where the risen Jesus is seen standing rather than seated at the Father's right hand, and Stephen sees it on his way to die for saying so. At this they covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him. They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him, and the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Luke drops the name into the story without comment, one line, the way a novelist plants a figure the whole rest of the book will follow. While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed the prayer of the cross in his own voice: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep. The first martyr dies asking mercy for his executioners, in words his Lord used before him, and the church outside Jerusalem begins here, scattered by the persecution this death opens, carrying the word with it.

title: The Gospel Comes to Samaria
subtitle: Acts 8:1–25
description: Persecution scatters the church into its second field; Philip preaches in Samaria, and Simon the sorcerer tries to buy the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen's death. Luke repeats the young man from the stoning so the next movement starts under his shadow: on that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him, while Saul began to destroy the church, going from house to house, dragging off men and women, and putting them in prison. The mission sentence of chapter 1 had named Judea and Samaria as the witnesses' second field. Persecution, not planning, is what sends them there: those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. The dispersion is the delivery system.

Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them. Philip, the second of the seven table-servers, preaching to Samaritans, the half-kin Israel had despised for centuries, in the first deliberate crossing of the book's map. The crowds all paid close attention to Philip's message and to the signs they saw him perform: with loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, and many of the paralyzed and lame were healed. So there was great joy in that city. Joy is Luke's fruit-word for the gospel arriving, and Samaria gets it before most of Judea does.

The city had a reigning wonder-worker already. A man named Simon had practiced sorcery there and astounded the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great, and all the people, from the least to the greatest, heeded his words and said, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power.” But when they believed Philip as he preached the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed and was baptized, and followed Philip closely, astounded now himself by the great signs and miracles he observed. The amazement trade had changed hands: the man who had made a career of astounding others walks around astounded.

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. On their arrival, they prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Luke reports the delay without explaining it: water first, the Spirit at the apostles' hands afterward, the mother church's witnesses physically present when Samaria is joined to the body, so that this first crossing would be sealed by Jerusalem itself and could never be read as a rival church starting across the border. The order is Luke's; the reason he leaves the reader to weigh.

When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money. “Give me this power as well,” he said, “so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” The old instinct prices the new gift. But Peter replied with the sharpest rebuke in the book so far: “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money! You have no part or share in our ministry, because your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of your wickedness, and pray to the Lord. Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart. For I see that you are poisoned by bitterness and captive to iniquity.” Even here, repentance is held open to the man who tried to purchase the Spirit, and Simon's answer is the most honest sentence he speaks: “Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing you have said may happen to me.” Luke leaves him there, asking for prayer, his end unwritten. And after Peter and John had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many of the Samaritan villages, the first two of the Twelve now evangelists in Samaria themselves. The border, once crossed by a scattered table-server, is now a road the apostles travel preaching.

title: What Prevents Me from Being Baptized?
subtitle: Acts 8:26–40
description: On a desert road, Philip opens Isaiah for Ethiopia's treasurer, and the ends of the earth believe in a single chariot.
paragraphs: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Get up and go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” Philip is pulled out of a Samaritan city ringing with joy and sent to a desert road with no crowd on it, and he goes without the reason. So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official in charge of the entire treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his return was sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah the prophet. Ethiopia, in the map of Luke's world, is the ends of the earth, and its treasurer is coming home from Jerusalem with a scroll he cannot yet read his way through, a God-fearer from the edge of the world asking questions in a chariot.

The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over to that chariot and stay by it.” So Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet, and asked the question that opens the whole encounter: “Do you understand what you are reading?” “How can I,” he said, “unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. The eunuch was reading this passage of Scripture: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth. In His humiliation He was deprived of justice. Who can recount His descendants? For His life was removed from the earth.” The treasurer of Ethiopia is parked, providentially, in the middle of Isaiah's suffering servant, the one passage in his prophets that asks its own question aloud. “Tell me,” said the eunuch, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. Luke does not give us the sermon. He gives us its starting point and its destination, a lamb silent before its shearers and the name of Jesus, and lets the reader who has read the Gospel connect them.

As they traveled along the road and came to some water, the eunuch said, “Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?” It is the right question from this particular man, because almost everything about him is a thing that had prevented people: a foreigner from the far south, a eunuch whose body barred him from the full assembly under the old law, a seeker who had worshiped at Jerusalem's edge. Philip's answer is the baptism itself. The eunuch gave orders to stop the chariot, and both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing. The treasurer loses his guide the moment the road forks and does not lose the joy; the gospel has reached the ends of the earth in one chariot, one conversion, no crowd, no city, just Scripture opened and water found in a desert. But Philip appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea. The evangelist walks home up the coast preaching, and Caesarea, the Roman capital on the sea, files his name away. The book will need that address again soon.

title: Saul, Saul
subtitle: Acts 9:1–19
description: The persecutor with warrants meets the risen Jesus on the Damascus road and is baptized by a disciple brave enough to call him brother.
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord. Luke's meanwhile reaches back across Samaria and the desert road to the young man who held the coats at the stoning, now gone to the high priest for paperwork: letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to the Way, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. The Way is the movement's first name for itself in this book, and Saul is hunting it with warrants, ninety miles of intent between him and Damascus.

As Saul drew near to Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” “Who are You, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied. “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” The accusation is the revelation: the hunted sect and the risen Jesus are one body as far as heaven is concerned, and persecuting the least disciple in Damascus is persecuting him. Luke will let Paul tell this story twice more in his own words, before a Jerusalem crowd and a king, and this series will tell it each time Luke tells it, because each telling is aimed at a different audience and carries details the others do not. The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless; they heard the voice but did not see anyone. Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could not see a thing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus. The hunter enters his hunting ground led like a child, and for three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything. The arrest he came to make has been made on him.

In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias, and the Lord spoke to him in a vision and called his name, and Ananias answered as Samuel and Isaiah answered. The Lord told him to get up and go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight. Ananias's objection is the most reasonable prayer in the book: “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem. And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” The Lord's answer is a command and a commissioning in one breath: “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel. I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” The whole second half of Acts is inside that sentence, Gentiles and kings and Israel, and its price tag is stated before its program: suffering, shown to him across a lifetime.

So Ananias went to the house, and when he arrived, he placed his hands on Saul, and the first word the church's great persecutor hears from the church is a family word: “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and his sight was restored. He got up and was baptized, and after taking some food, he regained his strength. The man who came to Damascus to chain believers is baptized in Damascus by a believer he came to chain, in the house of a man named Judas on the street called Straight, and Luke leaves the scene there, at a table, with food, strength returning. The conversion of Saul is the book's hinge, and it is handled with almost no machinery: a light, a voice, three blind days, and an ordinary disciple brave enough to say brother to his enemy.

title: A Basket Over the Wall
subtitle: Acts 9:20–31
description: Saul preaches in Damascus, escapes in a basket, is vouched for by Barnabas in Jerusalem, and the church enjoys a season of peace.
paragraphs: Saul promptly began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, declaring, “He is the Son of God.” Promptly is Luke's word and it deserves the emphasis: no apprenticeship, no waiting period, no committee. The warrant-carrier walks into the Damascus synagogues he came to police and preaches the opposite of his errand. All who heard him were astounded and asked, “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hasn’t he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?” But Saul was empowered all the more, and he confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ. The trained Pharisee's mind, turned around, is a weapon now aimed the other way, and Damascus is its first proving ground.

After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him, but Saul learned of their plot. Day and night they watched the city gates in order to kill him. One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall. His disciples: the persecutor has disciples of his own within the story's shortest span, and their first recorded act of discipleship is smuggling their teacher out of the city in a basket at night, the hunter leaving by the wall like a thief. Paul will tell this escape himself years later and add the detail Luke leaves out, that the governor's men were the ones watching the gates. Both tellings stand in this series where their books put them.

When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. The suspicion is honest and earned; Jerusalem remembers the house-to-house raids, and a conversion announced by its beneficiary is the oldest trick a persecutor could run. Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Barnabas, the Son of Encouragement, whose introduction to this book was selling a field, now spends something more valuable than land: his own credibility, staked on the most feared name in the church. He described how Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus. So Saul stayed with them, moving about freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord. He talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, his own old crowd, the freedmen's synagogues, but they tried to kill him. When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus, his home city, off the board for now. Jerusalem's peace is purchased by Saul's absence twice in one chapter, and the church learns to export its most dangerous convert for his own safety.

Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit. This is Luke's fourth great summary, and its geography is the mission map filling in: Judea, Galilee, Samaria at peace together, growing in strength and numbers at once, the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit named as the twin climates of the growth. The persecution that scattered the church has been survived; the persecutor who drove it is a brother in Tarsus; and the book now swings its camera back to Peter, traveling the countryside the peace has opened, because the next border to cross is bigger than Samaria, and Peter is the man who will be sent across it.

title: Tabitha, Get Up
subtitle: Acts 9:32–43
description: Peter heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa, staying on in the house of a tanner named Simon.
paragraphs: As Peter traveled throughout the area, he went to visit the saints in Lydda. The apostle of Pentecost is making rounds now, visiting the scattered congregations the persecution planted, and at Lydda he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. “Aeneas,” Peter said to him, “Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat.” Immediately Aeneas got up. Peter assigns the healing to Jesus Christ in the sentence itself, the same refusal of credit he made at the Beautiful Gate, and the whole region reads the result: all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. One man up from a mat of eight years, and the coastal plain turns.

In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which is translated as Dorcas, who was always occupied with works of kindness and charity. Luke gives her two names, Aramaic and Greek, the way he gives her one occupation: kindness, practiced with a needle. At that time, however, she became sick and died, and her body was washed and placed in an upper room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to urge him, “Come to us without delay.” The errand's urgency assumes what Joppa hoped and had not yet seen in this book: the dead might not have to stay dead when an apostle can be fetched in time.

So Peter got up and went with them. On his arrival, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them. The evidence presented at this deathbed is a wardrobe: garments made by hand for widows, held up one by one in a room full of crying women, the whole ministry of the woman on the bed itemized in cloth. It is the most tender exhibit in Acts, and Peter treats the moment the way his Lord treated a similar room in the Gospel Luke wrote: he sent them all out. Then Peter knelt down and prayed, and turning toward her body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. Two words in her own Aramaic, as near an echo of Jesus raising a ruler's daughter as language allows, and Luke reports the result in the order it happened: eyes, recognition, sitting up. Peter took her by the hand and helped her up. Then he called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive. The widows' evidence is returned to them with its maker inside it.

This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. And Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. The last line looks like lodging trivia and is quietly load-bearing. A tanner works with dead animals and their hides, an unclean trade that kept its practitioner at the edge of Jewish observance, and Peter is staying in his house, eating at his table, for days. The apostle to the circumcised is being housed one small step at a time outside the lines he grew up inside, and the next knock on that tanner's gate is coming from Caesarea, from a Roman officer's household, and Peter will need every step of the preparation Joppa has been giving him.

title: A Sheet Let Down from Heaven
subtitle: Acts 10:1–23
description: A Roman centurion's prayer is answered in Joppa, where a hungry Peter sees a sheet full of animals and hears a voice he argues with.
paragraphs: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was called the Italian Regiment. Caesarea is Rome's capital in Judea, all marble and garrison, and its Italian Regiment's centurion is introduced by his religion before his rank: he and all his household were devout and God-fearing. He gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly. One day at about the ninth hour, the hour of prayer Peter and John kept at the temple, he had a clear vision of an angel of God who came to him and called his name. Cornelius stared at him in fear and asked, “What is it, Lord?” The angel answered, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God. Now send men to Joppa to call for a man named Simon who is called Peter. He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.” Heaven's directions are almost comically practical: a name, a double name, a host, a landmark. Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his attendants, explained what had happened, and sent them to Joppa, thirty miles down the coast, to fetch a Jewish fisherman to a Roman officer's house.

The next day at about the sixth hour, as the men were approaching the city on their journey, Peter went up on the roof to pray. He became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. The timing is the teacher: God addresses Peter's table rules at the exact hour his stomach is empty. He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners. It contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air, clean and unclean together in one sailcloth of a vision. Then a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” “No, Lord!” Peter answered. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” It is one of the few places in Scripture where a man tells the Lord no and means it as obedience: Peter's whole life of kosher faithfulness rises up in the refusal. The voice spoke to him a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” This happened three times, and all at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven. Three times, for the apostle whose denials also came in threes, and Luke leaves the vision standing without an interpretation attached, because Peter does not have one yet either.

While Peter was puzzling over the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found Simon's house and approached the gate. They called out to ask if Simon called Peter was staying there. As Peter continued to reflect on the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. So get up! Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them.” The interpretation of the sheet arrives as people at a gate, which is how this book usually explains things. So Peter went down to the men and said, “Here am I, the one you are looking for. Why have you come?” “Cornelius the centurion has sent us,” they said. “He is a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation. A holy angel instructed him to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you.” So Peter invited them in as his guests. Gentile servants and a Roman soldier sleeping under the tanner's roof, eating the tanner's food, hosted by the apostle who an hour ago could not eat an unclean animal in a vision. The sheet's meaning is still unspoken, and Peter is already acting it. The next day he got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa, Jewish witnesses for a road no apostle had yet walked: into a Gentile's house, on purpose, at heaven's direction.

title: God Shows No Partiality
subtitle: Acts 10:24–48
description: Peter preaches in Cornelius's house, and the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles mid-sermon, before the water, before the vote.
paragraphs: The following day he arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. As Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet to worship him. But Peter helped him up. “Stand up,” he said, “I am only a man myself.” The first exchange at the gospel's first Gentile door is a correction of posture: the centurion's reverence refused by the fisherman's plain fact. As Peter talked with him, he went inside and found many people gathered together, a house full of Romans waiting on a sermon they had been summoned to by an angel and a dream, and Peter opens with the sheet's meaning now clear to him at last: “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean. So when I was invited, I came without objection. I ask, then, why have you sent for me?”

Cornelius answers with the whole story in one breath, four days back to his ninth-hour prayer, the man in radiant clothing, the words heaven spoke to him: “Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God.” Then the errand to Joppa, and the conclusion that is the finest definition of a congregation in the book: “So I sent for you immediately, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.” Then Peter began to speak, and his first sentence is the lesson the sheet was sent to teach, stated now as something he understands rather than something he was told: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right.”

The sermon that follows is the Gospel in outline, preached to people hearing it for the first time: “He has sent this message to the people of Israel, proclaiming the gospel of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.” Lord of all, in a Gentile's front room. Peter rehearses the story they partly know, “how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how Jesus went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him.” Then the witnesses' own credential: they saw all he did in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem; they put him to death by hanging him on a tree; “God raised Him up on the third day and caused Him to be seen,” he said, “not by all the people, but by the witnesses God had chosen beforehand, by us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead.” And the commission transferred: “He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead. All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”

Peter does not get to finish. While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message. All the circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles, for they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God.
