Pentecost repeats in a Roman living room, uninvited by the sermon and ahead of the baptism, heaven ratifying the border-crossing before the church can vote on it. Then Peter said the only thing left for the church to say: “Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!” So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days. The apostle who crossed the threshold stays for days at Gentile tables, and the six brothers from Joppa have seen everything with their own eyes, which will matter, because Jerusalem has heard that Peter went into the home of uncircumcised men and ate with them, and an explanation is going to be required.

title: First Called Christians
subtitle: Acts 11:1–30
description: Peter defends the Gentile mission in Jerusalem, nameless believers found the church at Antioch, and Barnabas fetches Saul from Tarsus.
paragraphs: The apostles and brothers throughout Judea soon heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him and said, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” The charge is not doctrine; it is table fellowship, and it is accurate. Peter does not defend himself with authority. But Peter began and explained to them the whole sequence of events, step by step, the way a witness testifies: I was in Joppa praying, the trance, the sheet, the voice, and his own objection included in the record. “No, Lord,” I said, “for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” But the voice spoke from heaven a second time, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” This happened three times. Then the arrival, timed to the minute: three men from Caesarea stopped at the house just as the vision ended. “The Spirit told me to accompany them without hesitation. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s home.” Note the six brothers in Peter's testimony: they are his corroborating witnesses, brought to Jerusalem as evidence, the Joppa men standing in the room while their apostle is questioned.

Cornelius's angel gets retold too, and his message, “He will convey to you a message by which you and all your household will be saved.” Then Peter reaches the moment his whole defense rests on: “As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning. Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how He said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?” Who was I to hinder God: the defense is that resistance, not compliance, would have been the disobedience. When they heard this, they had no further objections, and they glorified God, saying, “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.” Even the Gentiles: the wonder is still in their voices. The first theological crisis of the church is settled not by a decree but by a story told in sequence and a gift that arrived before the church's permission, and the settlement holds exactly as long as the parties involved; the question will be reopened later, under rougher conditions.

Meanwhile those scattered by the persecution that began with Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the message only to Jews. But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks as well, proclaiming the good news about the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord. Luke names no names for the founders of the church that will dominate the rest of his book: anonymous scattered Cypriots and Cyrenians, crossing the Jew-Greek line on their own initiative before any apostle authorized it, at Antioch in Syria, the empire's third city. When news of this reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Not an investigator with charges this time; Barnabas, the encourager. When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts, for Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.

Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he found him, he brought him back to Antioch. The man who vouched for Saul's conversion now rides north to recruit him: the church's growth has outrun its teachers, and Barnabas knows exactly one underused mind in Tarsus. So for a full year they met together with the church and taught large numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch, a nickname coined by the city, half joke no doubt, for people whose talk was all Christ; the movement now has a public name. In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem, and one named Agabus predicted through the Spirit that a great famine would sweep across the whole world, which happened under Claudius. So the disciples, each according to his ability, decided to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, sending their gifts to the elders with Barnabas and Saul. The youngest Gentile church's first corporate act is a famine offering to the mother church, carried by the pair who will carry the gospel west. Antioch gives money to Jerusalem. Before long it will give the world its missionaries, and the same two pairs of hands will be laid on for that too.

title: Peter Delivered, Herod Fallen
subtitle: Acts 12:1–25
description: Herod kills James and jails Peter; an angel walks Peter out past the guards, Rhoda forgets to open the gate, and Herod falls in Caesarea.
paragraphs: About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church. This is Herod Agrippa, grandson of the Herod who hunted Bethlehem's children, ruling a briefly reunited kingdom and courting the favor of Jerusalem's establishment. He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. One verse, no rescue, no angel, no explanation. James, son of Zebedee, one of the inner three, is the first apostle to die, and Luke gives his death less space than Peter's escape, because the book is not a ledger of fairness and does not pretend that prayer works by quota. And seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod proceeded to seize Peter also, during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each, sixteen men in rotation for one fisherman. Herod intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover: a public execution as a feast-week offering.

So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him. On the night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries standing guard at the entrance. Sleeping: the condemned apostle's last night is spent asleep between his guards, and the detail is worth keeping, because this is what the peace of the church's prayers looked like from inside the cell. Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He tapped Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his wrists. “Get dressed and put on your sandals,” said the angel. Peter did so, and the angel told him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” The rescue proceeds at a dresser's pace: get up, dress, sandals, cloak, follow. So Peter followed him out, but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real; he thought he was only seeing a vision, a reasonable assumption for the man who had seen a sheet full of animals on a rooftop. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city, which opened for them by itself. When they had gone outside and walked the length of one block, the angel suddenly left him. Then Peter came to himself and said, “Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s grasp and from everything the Jewish people were anticipating.”

And when he had realized this, he went to the house of Mary the mother of John, also called Mark, where many people had gathered together and were praying. He knocked at the outer gate, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer it. When she recognized Peter's voice, she was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate, but ran inside and announced, “Peter is standing at the gate!” “You are out of your mind,” they told her. But when she kept insisting it was so, they said, “It must be his angel.” It is the most human scene in Acts: the church is fervently praying for Peter's deliverance in the very house where the delivered man stands knocking, and the praying church will not believe the answer when a servant girl reports it. But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astounded. Peter motioned with his hand for silence, and he described how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. “Send word to James and to the brothers,” he said, and he left for another place. James here is the Lord's brother, rising now in the Jerusalem church; Peter exits Luke's story as its lead figure with a message left behind and no forwarding address, his work of founding done, the book's second half belonging to the man Barnabas fetched from Tarsus.

At daybreak there was no small commotion among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter. After Herod had searched for him unsuccessfully, he examined the guards and ordered that they be executed. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea. There, on an appointed day, Herod donned his royal robes, sat on his throne, and addressed the people of Tyre and Sidon, who had come begging peace because their region depended on the king's country for food. And they began to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!” Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. The king who killed an apostle and jailed another is struck down for accepting the worship Peter refused from Cornelius in this same city, and Luke sets the two scenes down without underlining them. But the word of God continued to spread and multiply. That is the chapter's true last word on kings and churches alike. When Barnabas and Saul had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem, they returned to Antioch, bringing with them John, also called Mark: the famine gift delivered by the two men the book is about to send out, with a young helper in tow whose name the reader should remember.

title: Set Apart for Me
subtitle: Acts 13:1–12
description: In a worshiping, fasting church at Antioch, the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul; on Cyprus a sorcerer goes blind and a governor believes.
paragraphs: Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. Read the list as a map of the movement's reach: a Cypriot Levite, a man whose nickname says Africa, a Cyrenian, a foster-brother of a Herod, and the Tarsus Pharisee, governing one congregation together. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” The first missionary sending in the book is not a church's strategy. It is a word given in worship, to a fasting congregation, naming its two most valuable men, including the man who had led the church's founding year. And after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off. Antioch loses its best and calls it obedience.

So Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus. Barnabas's home island is the first field, and the pattern of the whole journey sets in its first week: when they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues, synagogue first, city by city, for the rest of the book. And John was with them as their helper, John Mark, carried along from Jerusalem. They traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos, where they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, a man of intelligence, summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. Rome's governor on Cyprus asks for the sermon personally, and the sorcerer at his elbow can hear his livelihood ending.

But Elymas the sorcerer, for that is what his name means, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked directly at Elymas and said, and from this sentence forward Luke calls him Paul, his Roman name for a Roman-facing life: “O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness, you are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery! Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord? Now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. The blindness that fell on Saul on the Damascus road falls now, by Saul's own word, on the man blocking the road for someone else, temporary in both cases and instructional in both: the false prophet gropes for a hand the way the true apostle once did. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord. Luke is careful about the order: the sign astonished, but it was the teaching he believed. Cyprus is crossed, a governor believes, a sorcerer gropes, and the mission is seven verses old and already complete in miniature: word preached, power contested, sight traded, and the ends of the earth one island closer.

title: To the Gentiles
subtitle: Acts 13:13–52
description: Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch ends with the journey's charter: since you reject it, we turn to the Gentiles.
paragraphs: After setting sail from Paphos, Paul and his companions came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them to return to Jerusalem. Paul and his companions: the order of names has quietly reversed since Cyprus, and John Mark's departure gets one flat sentence and no explanation, a loose thread Luke will let Paul himself pull on years later at a dockside argument. From Perga they traveled inland to Pisidian Antioch, another Antioch, up in the Galatian highlands, where they entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down. After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.” Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and began to speak, and the sermon that follows is the fullest specimen of Paul's synagogue preaching Luke gives us, preserved because this series keeps speeches whole.

“Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!” The audience is named in its two parts from the first line, and the sermon walks the seam between them. Paul surveys the history Stephen surveyed, faster, with a different destination: God chose the fathers, made them great in Egypt, led them out with an uplifted arm, endured their conduct forty years in the wilderness, vanquished seven nations in Canaan, gave judges until Samuel, then Saul son of Kish for forty years. “After removing Saul, He raised up David as their king and testified about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.’ From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised.” John the Baptist gets his verse, with his own disclaimer quoted: “Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One. But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” Then Paul turns to the room: “Brothers, children of Abraham, and you Gentiles who fear God, it is to us that this message of salvation has been sent.”

Jerusalem did not recognize him, and in condemning him fulfilled the prophets read every Sabbath; though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him executed; they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. “But God raised Him from the dead, and for many days He was seen by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now His witnesses to our people.” And Paul argues the resurrection out of the same psalms Peter used at Pentecost, plus one: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.” “I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.” “You will not let Your Holy One see decay.” David served God's purpose in his own generation, fell asleep, was buried with his fathers, and saw decay; the One God raised did not see decay. Then the sermon's point lands, aimed at the seam in the room: “Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. Through Him everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.” And it ends with Habakkuk's warning like a held breath: “Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish! For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.”

As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath, and many of the Jews and devout converts followed them home, urged to continue in the grace of God. On the following Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they blasphemously contradicted what Paul was saying. Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly, in the sentence that becomes the journey's charter and the book's recurring hinge: “It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles. For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed. The Jews incited the prominent women and leading men of the city and drove the two out of their district, and Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium. And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit: expelled preachers, rejoicing converts, and the word spreading through the whole region behind them. The pattern of the journeys is now fully drawn, synagogue, sermon, split, expulsion, joy, and it will repeat in city after city.

title: They Called the Apostles Gods
subtitle: Acts 14:1–28
description: At Lystra a healed cripple brings sacrifice to the apostles, then stones Paul; the first journey closes with elders appointed in every church.
paragraphs: At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went as usual into the Jewish synagogue, where they spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers, and Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there anyway, speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of his grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders. The people of the city were divided, some siding with the Jews and others with the apostles, until a plot of Gentiles and Jews together with their rulers to mistreat and stone them was discovered, and they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding region, where they continued to preach the gospel. The journey's geography is now driven as much by expulsion as by planning, and Luke reports both without embarrassment.

In Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet, who was lame from birth and had never walked. This man was listening to the words of Paul, who looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. In a loud voice Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” And the man jumped up and began to walk. It is the Beautiful Gate healing mirrored in a pagan city, a man lame from birth on his feet at a word, but there is no temple here, no Scriptures in the crowd's head, and what happens next is what happens when a miracle lands on pure paganism with no framework to catch it. When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have come down to us in human form!” Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds. Local legend held that the gods had visited this region before in disguise and been refused; Lystra was not going to make that mistake twice, and the missionaries, who do not speak Lycaonian, nearly get worshiped before they understand a word of it.

But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out about this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting the most urgent sermon of the journey, preached against a sacrifice being offered to themselves: “Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them. In past generations, He let all nations go their own way. Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” To a crowd with no Bible, Paul preaches creation and providence, rain and harvest as God's standing witness, and even with these words, Paul and Barnabas could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them. The refusal of worship is becoming a signature of this book: Peter lifts Cornelius off his knees, Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes at Lystra, and Herod, who accepted the shout of a god, is eaten by worms. Luke has built the contrast piece by piece.

Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead. The same city that tried to sacrifice to Paul as a god stones him as a criminal within the same visit, on the word of men who traveled a hundred miles to arrange it; Luke records both verdicts without comment and lets them stand side by side as his whole commentary on crowds. But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. Back into the city, the same evening, on his own feet. And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, the whole hostile circuit, in reverse, on purpose: strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said. Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed. The first journey ends not with conquest but with organization: churches revisited, elders appointed, converts told plainly that hardship is the road and not a detour. After passing through Pisidia they came to Pamphylia, spoke the word in Perga, went down to Attalia, and sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had just completed. When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. The opened door is the journey's headline in the sending church's minutes, and it is precisely the door that men are about to travel up from Jerusalem to try to narrow.

title: The Council at Jerusalem
subtitle: Acts 15:1–35
description: The circumcision question is settled by testimony, prophecy, and a short letter: it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.
paragraphs: Then some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” The sentence arrives at Antioch without apostolic authorization, as Jerusalem's own letter will later admit, and it aims at the Gentile converts' standing itself: not advice about practice, but a condition on salvation. And after engaging these men in sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question. Sharp debate first, then a delegation: the church's way with its deepest disagreement is to argue it honestly and then carry it to the whole body. Sent on their way by the church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers, so the defendants tour the evidence on their way to the trial. On their arrival in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders, to whom they reported all that God had done through them. But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.”

So the apostles and elders met to look into this matter. After much discussion, Peter got up and said to them, and the order of speakers is Luke's own argument: the apostle of the sheet speaks first, and his testimony is Cornelius's house retold as doctrine. “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith. Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear? On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” Just as they are: the saved Jews and the saved Gentiles trade places in Peter's sentence, and the mother church's apostle ends by confessing that his own people's salvation runs on the same grace as the newcomers'. The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. Testimony, then silence, then Scripture.

When they had finished speaking, James declared. James the Lord's brother presides, and his ruling welds Peter's experience to Amos's prophecy: “Brothers, listen to me! Simon has told us how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people to be His own. The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David. Its ruins I will rebuild, and I will restore it, so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name, says the Lord who does these things that have been known for ages.’” David's fallen tent rebuilt, and the Gentiles streaming into it by name: James reads the Cornelius event and the Antioch churches as the prophets' own plot. “It is my judgment, therefore, that we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God. Instead, we should write and tell them to abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood. For Moses has been proclaimed in every city from ancient times and is read in the synagogues on every Sabbath.” Four abstentions, aimed at the table fellowship of mixed churches and the idol-feasts of pagan cities, and no circumcision, no law of Moses laid on the Gentiles as a yoke.

Then the apostles and elders, with the whole church, decided to select men from among them to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers, carrying the letter. The letter is quoted because it matters word for word: “It has come to our attention that some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.” The teachers are disowned before the teaching is answered. “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements: You must abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. You will do well to avoid these things. Farewell.” It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us: the council's authority claimed in one clause, heaven and the church deliberating in a single sentence. So the men were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they assembled the congregation and delivered the letter. When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message. Judas and Silas, who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers, and after some time were sent off in peace. But Paul and Barnabas remained at Antioch, along with many others, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. The question that could have split the church in its cradle is settled by testimony, prophecy, and a short letter, and the Gentile mission survives its first council. It will not be the last time the letter's terms are tested, but the book now turns west again, and its two great carriers are about to part over a young man named Mark.

title: Come Over and Help Us
subtitle: Acts 15:36–16:15
description: Paul and Barnabas part over Mark, Timothy is circumcised for the road, a Macedonian pleads in a vision, and Lydia's heart is opened at Philippi.
paragraphs: Some time later Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark. But Paul thought it best not to take him, because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work. Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company. The man who vouched for Saul when no one else would, and the man he vouched for, split over the young helper who had gone home from Perga, and Luke records the fracture without taking sides or smoothing it: their disagreement was so sharp. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, his home island, and Barnabas walks out of Luke's story with the deserter in tow, on his way to becoming, in time, the cousin who gets a second chance. But Paul chose Silas, the council's own envoy, a prophet and leader of the Jerusalem church, and left, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. Two teams leave Antioch where one was planned, and the mission doubles by dividing.

Paul came to Derbe and then to Lystra, where he found a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father. The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, so he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. The sentence needs to be read next to the council's letter in the team's luggage: the man who fought circumcision as a condition of salvation circumcises his new aide as a condition of access, so that no synagogue door closes before the sermon starts. Luke reports both acts in the same journey without feeling obliged to reconcile them, and they are not in contradiction in Paul's own terms: circumcision as a requirement for heaven, never; circumcision as a passport for a half-Greek missionary, yes. As they went from town to town, they delivered the decisions handed down by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the people to obey. So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.

After the Holy Spirit had prevented them from speaking the word in the province of Asia, they traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. And when they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them. So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. Two doors shut by the Spirit himself, Asia to the south and Bithynia to the north, and the team walks the corridor between them with no explanation given, Luke's plainest lesson in how this mission is actually directed: not by map but by permission, granted and withheld. During the night, Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. We: here, without announcement, the narrator steps into the story. Luke joins the party at Troas, and his pronouns will come and go for the rest of the book, present at Philippi, absent for years, present again on the last road to Jerusalem, a companion whose arrivals and departures the text never explains and this series never invents reasons for.

We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace, and the following day on to Neapolis. From there we went to the Roman colony of Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia, a city of veterans and Roman law, where Luke can find no synagogue to report. On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate along the river, where it was customary to find a place of prayer. After sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered there. Europe's first recorded congregation is a women's prayer meeting by a river, and among those listening was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message. And when she and her household had been baptized, she urged us, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us. The Macedonian man's plea is answered by a Macedonian woman's household, baptized whole, and the church of Philippi begins as a guest room in a businesswoman's house, with hospitality offered as a condition of being believed. It will become the warmest church in Paul's life, and it starts here, with opened heart, opened home.

title: Singing at Midnight
subtitle: Acts 16:16–40
description: A slave girl's deliverance lands Paul and Silas in the stocks; they sing, the earth shakes, and the jailer's household is baptized before dawn.
paragraphs: One day as we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who earned a large income for her masters by fortune-telling. This girl followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” She continued this for many days. The advertisement is accurate and the advertiser is a slave, owned twice over, by the spirit that speaks through her and by the men who collect her earnings. Eventually Paul grew so aggravated that he turned and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” And the spirit left her at that very moment. A true message from a false source is still refused, because the gospel in this book does not accept sponsorship from the powers it displaces, and the girl's freedom is her owners' bankruptcy.

When the girl's owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace. They brought them to the magistrates with a charge carefully dressed for a Roman colony: “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans to adopt or practice.” Nothing about the girl, nothing about the money; race and public order instead, the two charges a colonial court cannot ignore. The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods. And after striking them with many blows, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely. On receiving this order, he placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks. No trial, no names taken, no citizenship asked: the first European sermon tour ends its first week in the deepest cell of the Philippi jail.

About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. Luke gives the midnight cell one sentence and it has outlasted empires: beaten men, feet in stocks, singing, with an audience of prisoners listening in the dark. Suddenly a strong earthquake shook the foundations of the prison. At once all the doors flew open and everyone's chains came loose. When the jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, presuming that the prisoners had escaped, which under Roman discipline would have cost him the escapees' sentences and likely worse. But Paul called out in a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” The earthquake frees every prisoner and not one runs; the missionaries' staying becomes the jailer's rescue before his conversion is even mentioned. Calling for lights, the jailer rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” Then Paul and Silas spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house. At that hour of the night, the jailer took them and washed their wounds. And without delay, he and all his household were baptized. Then he brought them into his home and set a meal before them. So he and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe in God. Wounds washed by the man who had fastened the stocks, baptism in the night, a meal before dawn: the jailer's house runs the whole Christian course between midnight and morning.

When daylight came, the magistrates sent their officers with the order: “Release those men.” The jailer informed Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders to release you. Now you may go on your way in peace.” But Paul said to the officers, “They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” Paul holds his citizenship in reserve until it can do the young church the most good: a quiet release leaves the Philippi believers under the cloud of a criminal expulsion, but a public apology by the magistrates themselves establishes the missionaries as wronged citizens, and any future harassment of their converts will have to reckon with it. So the officers relayed this message to the magistrates, who were alarmed to hear that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens. They came to appease them and led them out, requesting that they leave the city. After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia's house to see the brothers and encourage them. Then they left the city. The colony that beat them unheard sends them off escorted by its own magistrates, and the church they leave behind meets in the purple-seller's house, founded in one week out of a riverside prayer meeting, a delivered slave girl, and a jailer's midnight household.

title: The World Turned Upside Down
subtitle: Acts 17:1–15
description: Thessalonica charges the missionaries with treason for naming another king, and the Bereans check the Scriptures daily to see if it is true.
paragraphs: When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ,” he declared. Three Sabbaths is all the time the pattern allows him here, and it is enough: some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women. The leading women keep appearing in Luke's Macedonian story, Lydia at the river, prominent wives in the synagogues, because Luke counts them part of the news.

The Jews, however, became jealous. So they brought in some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and sent the city into an uproar. They raided Jason's house in search of Paul and Silas, hoping to bring them out to the people. But when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other brothers before the city officials, shouting the charge that has followed this book around the world ever since: “These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here, and Jason has welcomed them into his home. They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus!” Another king, named Jesus: the accusation is the gospel stated as treason, and as a summary of what Paul had been preaching in their city it is, from the accusers' standpoint, not even unfair. On hearing this, the crowd and city officials were greatly disturbed. And they collected bond from Jason and the others and then released them, a financial muzzle on the host: your guests' message now has your money held against its peace. Luke does not hide the cost of hospitality in a hostile city; it is assessed in cash.

As soon as night had fallen, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. On arriving there, they went into the Jewish synagogue. Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true. More noble-minded is Luke's verdict, and the nobility is a method: eagerness without gullibility, the scrolls opened daily against the preacher's claims, checking the new thing by the old book in public. As a result, many of them believed, along with quite a few prominent Greek women and men. It is the only congregation in the journeys praised for how it listened, and this series, built on checking every quotation against its source, acknowledges a patron city when it meets one. But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea, they went there themselves to incite and agitate the crowds, traveling fifty miles to export their riot. The brothers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy remained in Berea. Those who escorted Paul brought him to Athens and then returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible. Paul travels on alone, escorted out of two cities in succession, and arrives in the intellectual capital of the world as a refugee from provincial mobs, which is not the worst preparation for what Athens will ask of him.

title: The Unknown God
subtitle: Acts 17:16–34
description: In Athens Paul preaches from an altar to an unknown god to the Areopagus, and a handful believe, including a member of the council.
paragraphs: While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also began to debate with him, the two reigning schools of the age, pleasure rightly ordered and virtue self-sufficient, and Athens's first review of the gospel is a shrug: “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign gods.” They said this because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection, which Athenian ears parsed as two new deities, Jesus and his consort Resurrection. So they took Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, the council hill of Mars, where the city once tried cases of blood and still vetted new teachings, and asked him with perfect Athenian politeness: “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears, and we want to know what they mean.” Now all the Athenians and foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas, Luke notes, in the driest parenthesis in the book. Paul has a hearing. It is also an entertainment booking, and he knows it.

Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, and the sermon that follows is the book's one full specimen of Paul preaching to educated pagans with no Scriptures in common: “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.” He starts from their own altar, their own admission of ignorance built in stone, and names the unknown. “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands. Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.” Stephen's temple argument returns in philosophical dress: the Maker is not housed, not fed, not needy. “From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands. God intended that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.” And Paul quotes their own poets the way he quoted Moses in the synagogue: “For in Him we live and move and have our being.” “We are His offspring.” “Therefore, being offspring of God, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination. Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent. For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.”

When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some began to mock him, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” The resurrection is where Athens divides, exactly where Jerusalem divided at the same word before the Sanhedrin: some mock, some defer, and a few cross over. At that, Paul left the Areopagus. But some joined him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, a member of the very council that heard him, a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them. No church is said to be founded, no return visit recorded; Luke's Athens harvest is a handful of named souls, the smallest yield in the journeys, reported without apology or excuse. The gospel that turned Thessalonica upside down in three Sabbaths gets a polite hearing and a few believers in the city that prided itself on hearing everything. Both results are in the record, side by side, and Luke lets the reader sit with the difference. Paul leaves for Corinth, a port city of sailors, slaves, and commerce, about as unlike Athens as a city can be, and it is Corinth, not Athens, that will keep him a year and a half.

title: Keep Speaking
subtitle: Acts 18:1–17
description: Paul works at a Corinth workbench for a year and a half under a vision's promise, and Gallio dismisses his case without hearing his defense.
paragraphs: After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them, and he stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was. The apostle takes up his trade again in a refugee couple's workshop: the man who addressed the Areopagus sews leather and canvas in Corinth, lodging with exiles, earning his keep, and reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike. The longest stay of the journeys begins at a workbench.

And when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ, the Macedonian churches' support having freed his hands from the bench. But when they opposed and insulted him, he shook out his garments and told them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. Next door: the transfer of venue is measured in feet, and the synagogue's own leader crossed them: Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. And many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent. For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” The promise names a harvest not yet gathered, many people in this city already counted as the Lord's before they have heard, and it sets the stay's length: So Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. Eighteen months of sermons get one sentence; the churches' long ordinary seasons are the journeys' load-bearing walls, and Luke builds them out of summaries on purpose.

While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. “This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law,” they said. But just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio told the Jews, “If this matter involved a wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, it would be reasonable for me to hear your complaint. But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.” And he drove them away from the judgment seat. Paul never opens his mouth in his own defense; Rome's newest proconsul dismisses the case as a theological squabble beneath the court's notice, and the dismissal does quiet legal work for the whole empire: in Achaia at least, the gospel is a dispute about words and names inside Judaism, not a crime. At this, the crowd seized Sosthenes the synagogue leader and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this was of concern to Gallio. Luke's last line on the episode is a shrug recorded for the ages: the synagogue leader beaten under the bench, the proconsul unmoved, the vision's promise kept in a courtroom where the defendant never had to speak. Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers. The year and a half and then some, in the city the philosophers' city would have pitied, becomes the journeys' longest pulpit so far.

title: Apollos
subtitle: Acts 18:18–28
description: Priscilla and Aquila take an eloquent Alexandrian aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and Apollos sails to Achaia with a letter.
paragraphs: Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers. He had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made, and then he sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. Luke mentions the vow in passing and explains none of it, a private act of Jewish devotion by the apostle of Gentile freedom, filed without commentary because in Luke's world the two were never the contradiction later ages made of them. When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a while longer, he declined. But as he left, he said, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” And he set sail from Ephesus. When Paul had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church at Jerusalem. Then he went down to Antioch. After Paul had spent some time in Antioch, he traveled from place to place throughout the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. The second journey closes in a rush of geography, and the third opens in a single sentence, because Luke's subject in these verses is not the travel. It is what he left behind in Ephesus: a tentmaking couple and a promise.

Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and was fervent in spirit. He spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. The portrait is generous and exact at once: eloquence, learning, fervor, accuracy, and one gap. Apollos preaches a true Jesus with an outdated baptism, John's water of repentance without the Spirit's arrival at Pentecost, a disciple of the forerunner's school still teaching on the far side of the events that completed it. And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. The correction is a model of how this book handles a gifted man's gap: not a public refutation, not a sermon against him, but a couple taking him aside, privately, at their own table presumably, a tentmaker and his wife instructing an Alexandrian scholar, and the scholar's eloquence survives the lesson because his teachability exceeds it. Luke names Priscilla before Aquila in the sentence, as he does in most of their mentions.

When Apollos resolved to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed. For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. The man who arrived in Ephesus with half the map leaves it with a letter of recommendation and becomes Corinth's powerhouse debater, the very city Paul is heading back toward by the long road through Galatia. Apollos will matter to the Corinthian church almost too much, as Paul's later letters complain about factions forming around his name, but Luke's portrait stays warm and unbothered: eloquent, instructed, fervent, corrected, sent. Ephesus is now stocked and waiting, a synagogue visited, a couple planted, a scholar dispatched, and a promise outstanding: I will come back to you if God is willing. The next chapter opens with the willing God keeping it, and with Apollos's old gap, John's baptism, waiting for Paul in the first men he meets.

title: The Riot at Ephesus
subtitle: Acts 19:1–41
description: Two years in Tyrannus's hall, a fortune in magic books burned, and a silversmith's riot that a city clerk dissolves; Paul resolves to see Rome.
paragraphs: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the interior and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples and asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” “No,” they answered, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” “Into what, then, were you baptized?” Paul asked. “The baptism of John,” they replied. Here is Apollos's gap in twelve men at once, about twelve men in all, a pocket of the forerunner's movement surviving years past its completion. Paul explained: “John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.” On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Luke's sequence of the Spirit's arrivals now has its fourth panel, and this series keeps the locking order he gives them: Pentecost's crowd, Samaria's delay, Cornelius's mid-sermon fall, and now disciples of John completed by Paul's hands, each arrival in its own shape, none of them smoothed into a system.

Then Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God. But when some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way, Paul took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord. A rented hall, daily discussions, two years: Ephesus is not a tour stop but a headquarters, and the whole province hears the word out of one classroom. God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and the diseases and evil spirits left them. Work aprons from the tentmaking bench carried to sickbeds; Luke calls the miracles extraordinary, as if marking that even by his book's standards this season runs hot.

Now there were some itinerant Jewish exorcists who tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those with evil spirits. They would say, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this. But one day the evil spirit responded, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded. The borrowed name fails at the exact point of borrowing: hell recognizes its adversaries personally, and secondhand authority is no authority. This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus, and fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor. Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds. And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. When the value of the books was calculated, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas, a fortune in wages voluntarily incinerated by converts cleaning house. So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail.

After these things had happened, Paul resolved in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. “After I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.” The book's last arc is announced in one sentence of itinerary: Jerusalem first, then Rome, and everything from here to the final chapter is that road. About that time there arose a great disturbance about the Way. It began with a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, bringing much business to the craftsmen. Demetrius assembled the craftsmen, along with the workmen in related trades. “Men,” he said, “you know that this business is our source of prosperity. And you can see and hear that not only in Ephesus, but in nearly the whole province of Asia, this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away. He says that man-made gods are no gods at all. There is danger not only that our business will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed,” he warned, “she who is worshiped by all the province of Asia and the whole world.” The speech is honest economics wearing religious dress, and it is also the gospel's finest backhanded review: nearly the whole province of Asia, persuaded to turn away, by one man in a lecture hall. When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

Soon the whole city was in disarray. They rushed together into the theatre, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia. Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him. Even some of Paul's friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre. Meanwhile the assembly was in turmoil. Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there. Luke's single driest crowd observation stands here: a riot of thousands, most of it ignorant of its own occasion. The Jews in the crowd pushed Alexander forward to explain himself, and he motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people. But when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Two hours of chanting is Luke's measurement, religion as endurance event. Finally the city clerk quieted the crowd and declared, “Men of Ephesus, doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven? Since these things are undeniable, you ought to be calm and not do anything rash. For you have brought these men here, though they have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess. So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there.” And the clerk's final argument is Rome, the fear that actually settles crowds in this book: “For we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events, and we have no justification to account for this commotion.” After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly. The riot dissolves on a clerk's voice, no soldiers, no arrests, two companions dragged in and released by adjournment. Paul's farewell to Ephesus will have to happen at a distance, on a beach at Miletus, and it is next.

title: You Will Not See My Face Again
subtitle: Acts 20:1–38
description: Eutychus falls and is restored at Troas, and on the beach at Miletus Paul charges Ephesus's elders and kneels with them in tears.
paragraphs: When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. And after encouraging them, he said goodbye to them and left for Macedonia. After traveling through that area and speaking many words of encouragement, he arrived in Greece, where he stayed three months. And when the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia. The traveling company is listed with hometowns attached, Sopater from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia: delegates of the churches, carrying the collection for Jerusalem's poor along the road with them. These men went on ahead and waited for us in Troas. Us: the narrator is back. Luke rejoins the party at the seam where he left it seven years before in the story's time, at Philippi where his we last spoke, and the pronoun returns without ceremony, as it always does. And after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi, and five days later we rejoined them in Troas, where we stayed seven days.

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight. Now there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. And a certain young man named Eutychus, seated in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead. The longest sermon in the book has a casualty, and Luke reports it without blaming the preacher's length or the boy's seat. But Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and embraced him. “Do not be alarmed!” he said. “He is still alive!” Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. And after speaking until daybreak, he departed. And the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive. The service that death interrupted simply resumes, through the meal, to dawn, and the congregation's souvenir is a living boy instead of a funeral.

We went on ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard. He had arranged this because he was going there on foot, walking the coast road alone for a day while his company sailed around the cape. And when he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene, then opposite Chios, then Samos, then Miletus. Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in the province of Asia, because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost. From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church. He will not go up to the city, the riot's memory and the schedule both forbidding, so the city comes down to the harbor, thirty miles, and Luke preserves the farewell address whole, the only speech in Acts addressed entirely to Christians, a pastor's charge rather than an evangelist's sermon.

When they came to him, he said, “You know how I lived the whole time I was with you, from the first day I arrived in the province of Asia. I served the Lord with great humility and with tears, especially in the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews. I did not shrink back from declaring anything that was helpful to you as I taught you publicly and from house to house, testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.” The defense of his ministry comes first, because the address is a deposit being handed over. “And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there. I only know that in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me. But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus,” he said, “the ministry of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.” Then the sentence the beach will remember: “Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men. For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God.”

“Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock. Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. Therefore be alert and remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears. And now I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified.” The charge runs watch, remember, wake: the shepherds are warned about wolves outside and wolves within, and the flock is commended not to the elders' strength but to God and the word of his grace. “I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions. In everything, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” It is the only saying of Jesus in this book that appears in no Gospel, preserved by Paul at a harbor farewell and by Luke in writing it here. When Paul had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed. They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him. They were especially grieved by his statement that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship. The presbyters of Ephesus walk their apostle to the water like family at a dock, and the book does not bring them face to face again.

title: The Mob at the Temple
subtitle: Acts 21:1–36
description: Warnings follow Paul up the coast; Agabus binds himself with Paul's belt, James proposes a vow, and a mob drags Paul out of the temple.
paragraphs: After we had torn ourselves away from them, we sailed directly to Cos, and the next day on to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. Tearing is Luke's word for the dock at Miletus, and the sailing that follows is a straight run down the coast with the warnings accumulating at every port. Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail. After sighting Cyprus and passing south of it, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo. We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. Through the Spirit: Luke says the Tyre church's warning is Spirit-given, while Paul has already said the Spirit compels him to go, and the text holds both sentences without harmonizing them, the way this book holds its prophet and its apostle on a collision course both calling it the Spirit's word. But when our time there had ended, we set out on our journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, accompanied us out of the city and knelt down on the beach to pray with us. And after we had said our farewells, we went aboard the ship, and they returned home. Whole families on the sand at Tyre, praying a man toward the chains he has been promised, in the same posture the Ephesian elders took at Miletus.

When we had finished our voyage from Tyre, we landed at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day. Leaving the next day, we went on to Caesarea and stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven. The table-server of the Jerusalem food line, the evangelist of Samaria and the desert road, is now a settled householder in the Roman capital with a house full of daughters: he had four unmarried daughters who prophesied, Joel's promise still running in the second generation. After we had been there several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea, the same prophet whose famine prediction had sent Antioch's offering north years before. Coming over to us, he took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’” The prophecy is theater, an Old Testament sign-act performed with a traveler's belt, and its terms are exact: bound by Jews, handed to Gentiles. When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. Luke counts himself among the pleaders, we pleaded, the narrator inside the argument and losing it. Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” When he would not be dissuaded, we quieted down and said, “The Lord’s will be done.” The company surrenders its counsel in the words of Gethsemane and of the Lord's own prayer, and packs.

When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully. The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present. Paul greeted them and recounted one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. When they heard this, they glorified God. Then they said to Paul, “You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law. But they are under the impression that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or observe our customs.” The rumor is stated precisely so the reader can judge it: Paul taught Gentiles they need not become Jews; the rumor converts it into Paul teaching Jews to abandon Moses. “What then should we do? They will certainly hear that you have come. Therefore do what we advise you. There are four men with us who have taken a vow. Take these men, purify yourself along with them, and pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that there is no truth to these rumors about you, but that you also live in obedience to the law. As for the Gentile believers, we have written to them our decision that they must abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality.” James quotes the council's decree back as settled law for the Gentiles while asking Paul for a public act of Jewish observance, both halves of the Jerusalem settlement performed by their original authors in one room. So the next day Paul took the men and purified himself along with them. Then he entered the temple to give notice of the date when their purification would be complete and the offering would be made for each of them.

When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul at the temple. The province of Asia: Ephesus's own Jews, who know his face from three years of synagogues and the Tyrannus hall, and who carry the grievance of the Demetrius season in person. They stirred up the whole crowd and seized him, crying out, “Men of Israel, help us! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people and against our law and against this place. Furthermore, he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place.” For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they assumed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Assumed: Luke flags the mob's central fact as a guess. The charge that will occupy Roman courts for two years rests on an assumption about a man seen in a street. The whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. While they were trying to kill him, the commander of the Roman regiment received a report that all Jerusalem was in turmoil. Immediately he took some soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. The commander came up and arrested Paul, ordering that he be bound with two chains. Agabus's belt, fulfilled on the temple steps within the week, two chains, Jerusalem binding, Gentile custody. Then he asked who he was and what he had done. Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, and some another. And since the commander could not get at the truth because of the uproar, he ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the mob. For the crowd that followed him kept shouting, “Away with him!” Rome's rescue is the mob's failure, and the prisoner is carried up the fortress steps like cargo, alive because an empire's garrison happened to be watching the temple courts from above. What he does at the top of those steps, turns around and asks to address the crowd that was just beating him, is the next episode, and it begins the long series of defenses that fill the rest of the book.

title: I Am a Roman Citizen
subtitle: Acts 21:37–22:29
description: From the fortress steps Paul tells Jerusalem his story in Hebrew until one word, Gentiles, breaks the hearing; his citizenship stops the flogging.
paragraphs: As they were about to take Paul into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” “Do you speak Greek?” he replied. “Aren’t you the Egyptian who incited a rebellion some time ago and led four thousand members of the Assassins into the wilderness?” The commander has the wrong file entirely: an Egyptian insurrectionist with four thousand knife-men is who Rome thinks it has arrested. But Paul answered, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city. Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people.” Having received permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd. A great hush came over the crowd, and he addressed them in Hebrew, the language of the temple and the Scriptures, and when they heard him speak to them in Hebrew, they became even more quiet. The man they had been beating as a defiler of the holy place addresses them in the holy tongue, from the fortress steps, under Roman escort, and the mob becomes an audience. “Brothers and fathers, listen now to my defense before you.”

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers. I was just as zealous for God as any of you are today. I persecuted this Way even to the death, detaining both men and women and throwing them into prison, as the high priest and the whole Council can testify about me.” Paul's defense is his biography, and its first movement establishes that his credentials outrun his accusers': Gamaliel's pupil, zealot, persecutor with council letters, one of their own at his most severe. This is the Damascus story's second telling in this book, and it is shaped for this audience: Ananias will be introduced not as a disciple but as a devout observer of the law, highly regarded by all the Jews in Damascus, and the commission will come wrapped in temple prayer. “About noon as I was approaching Damascus, suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me. I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?’ ‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting,’ He replied.” Of Nazareth: the name the indictment at his arrest kept using, planted by Paul himself inside the voice from heaven. “My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me.” In the first telling, the companions heard the voice but saw no one; here they see the light but cannot understand the voice. Luke lets both accounts stand in his own book without reconciling them, and this series does the same: two tellings of one event, each emphasizing what its moment needed, the seam left visible the way Luke left it.

“Then I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ ‘Get up and go into Damascus,’ He told me. ‘There you will be told all that you have been appointed to do.’” Ananias came and stood beside him. “Brother Saul,” he said, “receive your sight.” And at that moment I could see him. “Then he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will and to see the Righteous One and to hear His voice. You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard. And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’” Then Paul adds the part of the story only this telling carries, set years later in this same temple: praying at the temple, he fell into a trance and saw the Lord saying to him, “Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me.” “‘Lord,’ I answered, ‘they know very well that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You. And when the blood of Your witness Stephen was shed, I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ Then He said to me, ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

The crowd listened to Paul until he made this statement. Gentiles is the word the speech breaks on, the temple vision's whole destination, and Jerusalem's answer to it is instantaneous: then they lifted up their voices and shouted, “Rid the earth of him!
