He is not fit to live!” As they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air, the commander ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. He directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated to determine the reason for this outcry against him, Rome's standard shortcut to a prisoner's file. But as they stretched him out to strap him down, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?” The question is timed to the straps: not announced at the arrest, not pleaded at the beating the mob gave him, but deployed at the precise moment it converts his interrogators into defendants. On hearing this, the centurion went and reported it to the commander. “What are you going to do?” he said. “This man is a Roman citizen.” The commander went to Paul and asked, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he answered. “I paid a high price for my citizenship,” said the commander. “But I was born a citizen,” Paul replied. At once those who were about to interrogate Paul stepped back, and the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains. The Egyptian file closes. Rome has a citizen in chains, a mob it cannot satisfy, and an accusation it still cannot get stated in a form it understands, so the commander reaches for the one court that can translate the charges for him, and orders the Sanhedrin to assemble in the morning.

title: Forty Men Swore an Oath
subtitle: Acts 22:30–23:35
description: Paul splits the Sanhedrin on resurrection, a nephew exposes the ambush, and 470 soldiers carry him by night to Caesarea with Lysias's letter.
paragraphs: The next day the commander, wanting to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews, released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and had him stand before them. Paul looked directly at the Sanhedrin and said, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” At this, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck.” But those standing nearby said, “How dare you insult the high priest of God!” “Brothers,” Paul replied, “I was not aware that he was the high priest, for it is written: ‘Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.’” Luke leaves the exchange unexplained, whether Paul's eyes, ruined since Damascus perhaps, failed to pick out the high priest's robes, or the apology carries an edge the room would have heard. The text does not say, and this series does not choose. The hearing, such as it is, has barely opened and it is already blows and apologies.

Then Paul, knowing that some of them were Sadducees and the others Pharisees, called out in the Sanhedrin, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” As soon as he had said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. For the Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Paul's sentence is not a dodge in his own accounting; resurrection is precisely his hope, the axis of every sermon Luke has recorded for him. But its effect in that room is surgical: his trial becomes their schism. A great clamor arose, and some scribes from the party of the Pharisees got up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” The dispute grew so violent that the commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered the soldiers to go down and remove him by force and bring him into the barracks. Paul is rescued from his own defense by Roman infantry for the second time in two days, and the Sanhedrin hearing ends with the defendant extracted and the court debating itself. The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.” In the barracks, in chains, with his case unheard and his court dissolved, the prisoner is given the book's destination as a promise: Rome is no longer Paul's ambition of chapter 19. It is the Lord's appointment.

When daylight came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. More than forty of them were involved in this plot. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves with a solemn oath not to eat anything until we have killed Paul. Now then, you and the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring him down to you on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. We are ready to kill him on the way.” The plan needs the council's cooperation and the commander's routine, and it might have had both, except for the one relative Luke has never mentioned before: but when the son of Paul's sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul. Paul has a sister in Jerusalem, and a nephew with access and nerve, and the family's single appearance in the book is this errand. Then Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.” The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked, “What do you need to tell me?” He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of acquiring more information about him. Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him; they are ready now, awaiting your consent.” So the commander dismissed the young man and instructed him, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.” The oath of forty assassins is never heard of again in the book. What they ate, and when, Luke does not record.

Then he called two of his centurions and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea in the third hour of the night. Provide mounts for Paul to take him safely to Governor Felix.” Four hundred and seventy soldiers for one prisoner: the commander is not taking the ambush's measure lightly, and he writes the file's final document, a letter that Luke quotes whole: “This man was seized by the Jews, and they were about to kill him when I came with my troops to rescue him. For I had learned that he is a Roman citizen, and since I wanted to understand their charges against him, I brought him down to their Sanhedrin. I found that the accusation involved questions about their own law, but there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. When I was informed that there was a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once.” The letter's one creative touch is its chronology: Lysias implies the citizenship was learned before the rescue, when Luke's own narrative had the commander learn it at the flogging straps, after the chains were already on. A cover letter revising its author's mistakes is a thoroughly human document, and Luke includes it without a footnote. So the soldiers followed their orders and brought Paul by night to Antipatris. The next day they returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with him. When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul to him. The governor read the letter and asked what province Paul was from. Learning that he was from Cilicia, he said, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium, the palace of the Herod who ate worms in this same city in a chapter long past, now a Roman courthouse and prison. Paul is out of Jerusalem alive, in the custody of an empire that cannot figure out what he is accused of, with the Lord's sentence hanging over the rest of the book: you must testify in Rome.

title: I Appeal to Caesar
subtitle: Acts 24:1–25:12
description: Before Felix the case dissolves into adjournment and bribery hopes; before Festus, Paul exercises a citizen's right and appeals to Caesar.
paragraphs: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented to the governor their case against Paul. Jerusalem hires counsel for the rematch, and Tertullus opens with the period's standard flattery: “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation. In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this with all gratitude.” Felix's administration was notorious in its own day for the opposite, and Luke lets the lawyer's compliment sit unexamined, the way a reader of court speeches learns to discount the first paragraph. Then the indictment: “We have found this man to be a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and he even tried to desecrate the temple; so we seized him.” And then the lawyer's invitation: “By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all our charges against him.” Pestilence, ringleader, desecration: three charges, none of them the assumption about Trophimus stated in plain words, and the Jews present concurred, asserting that these charges were true.

When the governor motioned for Paul to speak, he began his response: “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense. You can verify for yourself that no more than twelve days ago I went up to Jerusalem to worship.” Twelve days: five of them this week in custody, seven in Jerusalem, the whole case compressed into a fortnight a governor can check. His accusers did not find him debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city, nor can they prove any of their charges. Then Paul volunteers the confession the prosecution never quite managed to state: “I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. In this hope, I strive always to maintain a clear conscience before God and man.” The defense is a mirror: the Way is not a departure from Israel's faith but its hope confessed, resurrection included, and the accusers cherish the same hope themselves. “After several years, then, I returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to my people and to present offerings.” Alms, the collection, named plainly: the prisoner's actual errand in the city was charity for the accusers' own people. At the time they found him in the temple, he was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar. But there are some Jews from the province of Asia who ought to appear before you and bring charges, if they have anything against me, the original witnesses, conveniently absent from their own prosecution. Otherwise, let these men state for themselves any crime they found in me when I stood before the Sanhedrin, “unless it was this one thing I called out as I stood in their presence: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

Then Felix, who was well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing and said, “When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case.” Lysias never comes; the adjournment is the verdict of a governor who knows enough about the Way to know the prisoner is harmless and enough about Jerusalem to know acquitting him costs more than delaying. He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs. After several days, Felix returned with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.” The governor keeps the preacher as a private chaplain he is afraid of, summoning him frequently, Luke notes, at the same time hoping that Paul would offer him a bribe: conscience and commerce in one audience chamber, and two years of both. After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. The book's plainest sentence on political justice: a man held two years without a charge proved, bequeathed to the next governor as a favor owed.

Three days after his arrival in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, where the chief priests and Jewish leaders presented their case against Paul. They urged Festus to grant them a concession against Paul by summoning him to Jerusalem, because they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way. The ambush is new, the tactic two years old: Jerusalem's leadership asks the new governor for the transfer the forty oath-men once needed, and Luke notes the murder scheduled underneath the paperwork without emphasis. But Festus replied, “Paul is being held in Caesarea, and I myself am going there soon. So if this man has done anything wrong, let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there.” The next day, in Caesarea, he sat on the judgment seat and ordered that Paul be brought in. When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove. Then Paul made his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.” But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?” The favor is the same favor Felix left the prisoner for, offered now as a venue change. Paul replied with the sentence the whole book has been traveling toward: “I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to their accusations against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!” Then Festus conferred with his council and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!” The appeal is a citizen's right and a one-way door: the case leaves provincial hands for the Emperor's court, and the road to Rome, promised in a barracks at night two years before the promise had a mechanism, now has one. What remains is for the empire to figure out what to write on the prisoner's file, and for that, Festus needs an expert. A king is coming to town.

title: Before Agrippa
subtitle: Acts 25:13–26:32
description: Paul's longest defense retells Damascus to a king, Festus cries madness, Agrippa asks about a short persuasion, and the verdict is innocence.
paragraphs: After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. Agrippa the Second, great-grandson of the Herod of Bethlehem, son of the Herod who killed James and died at Caesarea accepting worship, rules a northern kingdom and supervises the temple's affairs; his sister Bernice travels with him, as she travels with him everywhere, and Luke's introduction of the pair is a single courtly sentence that assumes the reader knows the family's weather. Since they were staying several days, Festus laid out Paul's case before the king: “There is a certain man whom Felix left in prison.” The Roman file on Paul, as Festus summarizes it for royalty, contains the book's most dryly accurate sentence about its own story: “They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive.” Festus had offered the prisoner a Jerusalem trial; Paul had appealed to Caesar; and now the governor's problem is paperwork. Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” “Tomorrow you will hear him,” Festus declared.

The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, along with the commanders and leading men of the city. And Festus ordered that Paul be brought in. Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man. The whole Jewish community has petitioned me about him, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer. But I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he has now appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him. I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry I may have something to write. For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him.” The hearing's purpose is openly clerical: the empire needs a charge sheet, and the king is its resident expert on the religion the charges keep dissolving into. Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense, the longest and most personal of his speeches in the book, delivered in chains to a court assembled as entertainment and retained as jurisprudence.

“King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to stand before you today to defend myself against all the accusations of the Jews, especially since you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies. I beg you, therefore, to listen to me patiently.” All the Jews know how he lived from childhood, a Pharisee of the strictest sect, and if his old colleagues are willing, they can testify to it themselves. “And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers, the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see fulfilled as they earnestly serve God day and night. It is because of this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews. Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” No charges are answered in this defense at all, because Paul has correctly identified the actual question in the room, and it is resurrection. His past is confessed at its worst: “So then, I too was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. And that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them.” The vote is a detail only this telling carries, as is the raging fury, the synagogue punishments, the attempt to make the saints blaspheme, persecution exported to foreign cities. And this pursuit is what had him on the Damascus road at noon.

“About noon, O king, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and my companions. We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice say to me in Hebrew, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’” The goads are new to this third telling, a farmer's proverb from the Lord's own mouth: the ox kicking the stick that guides it wounds only itself. And in this telling the commission comes whole on the road, not mediated through Ananias days later as the first account gave it: “‘But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you. I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’ So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.” Luke tells the conversion three times and harmonizes none of them: the goads appear here, the temple trance appeared in Jerusalem's version, Ananias's law-observance was for the crowd on the steps. Each audience got the telling shaped to it, and Luke preserves all three shapings without apology, which is why this series has done the same. “First to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, then to everyone in the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, I declared that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance. For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple courts and tried to kill me. But I have had God’s help to this day, and I stand here to testify to small and great alike. I am saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen: that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.”

At this stage of Paul's defense, Festus exclaimed in a loud voice, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” But Paul answered, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety. For the king knows about these matters, and I can speak freely to him. I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” And then Paul does what no defendant's handbook advises: he cross-examines the judge. “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” Then Agrippa said to Paul, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” The sentence is the most debated shrug in the book, somewhere between amusement and unease, and Luke leaves its tone for the reader's ear. “Short time or long,” Paul replied, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.” It is the defense's true conclusion: not acquittal requested, but conversion, of the king, the governor, the court, the whole auditorium, with the chains lifted in the gesture of a man showing them as he speaks. Then the king and the governor rose, along with Bernice and those seated with them. On their way out, they said to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.” The expert has spoken, the file is complete, and its verdict is innocence; the appeal, Paul's own act, is the only chain Rome did not forge. The prisoner sails for Rome as an innocent man under guard, which is exactly what the Lord in the barracks said would happen, in the order he said it: testified in Jerusalem, testified in Rome. What remains is the sea.

title: The Storm
subtitle: Acts 27:1–44
description: A prison ship sails into the Northeaster; fourteen days of storm end with bread given thanks for, a sandbar, and all 276 brought safely to land.
paragraphs: When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment. We are back: Luke's pronoun returns for the voyage and stays to the book's end, the narrator aboard the prison ship as a passenger in Paul's company. We boarded an Adramyttian ship about to sail for ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us, the man dragged into the Ephesus theatre years before, now traveling with the prisoner as far as Rome itself. The next day we landed at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care. The centurion's kindness is the voyage's first fact and its last rescue will depend on it. After putting out from there, we sailed to the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us, and across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia to Myra in Lycia, where the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board: a grain freighter of the great Egyptian fleet, big enough for two hundred seventy-six souls and a cargo of wheat.

After sailing slowly for many days, we arrived off Cnidus. When the wind impeded us, we sailed to the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone, and with difficulty along the coast to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea. By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast, past the Day of Atonement, deep into the season when Mediterranean sailing closes. So Paul advised them, “Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well.” But contrary to Paul's advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship. Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to sail on, hoping to reach Phoenix, a better harbor up the coast. It is the book's most democratic disaster: a majority vote, professional advice, a centurion outvoted by his own experts, and a prisoner overruled. When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had their opportunity. So they weighed anchor and sailed along, hugging the coast of Crete.

But it was not long before a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island. Unable to head into the wind, the ship was caught up. So we gave way and let ourselves be driven along. Passing to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we barely managed to secure the lifeboat. After hoisting it up, the crew used ropes to undergird the ship, passing cables around the hull to hold it together, and fearing the sandbars of Syrtis off Africa, they lowered the sea anchor and were driven along. We were tossed so violently that the next day the men began to jettison the cargo. On the third day, they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the great storm continued to batter us, we abandoned all hope of being saved. Luke the physician includes himself in the despair: we abandoned hope, the narrator with the sailors. The ship is now a drifting argument against ever having left Fair Havens, fourteen days of it, and the prisoner is the only man aboard whose information improves as conditions worsen.

After the men had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss. But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship. For just last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me. However, we must run aground on some island.” The I-told-you-so lasts one sentence and is spent on credibility for the promise; the promise itself is Caesar, the ship lost, every life granted, the grants attached to Paul's presence the way the jailer's household hung on his staying. On the fourteenth night we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea. About midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land. They took soundings and found twenty fathoms, then a little farther, fifteen fathoms. Fearing the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak, professional pagans praying in the dark with the rest of them.

Meanwhile, the sailors attempted to escape from the ship. Pretending to lower anchors from the bow, they let the lifeboat down into the sea. But Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” So the soldiers cut the ropes to the lifeboat and set it adrift. The promise has conditions and Paul enforces them like an officer: God has granted all lives, and the sailors must be aboard for the grant to work on them, so the escape boat goes empty. Right up to daybreak, Paul kept urging them all to eat: “Today is your fourteenth day in constant suspense, without taking any food. So for your own preservation, I urge you to eat something, because not a single hair of your head will be lost.” After he had said this, Paul took bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat. A prisoner presides at the last supper of the voyage, giving thanks before two hundred seventy-six frightened men, and Luke uses the grammar of the Lord's table and the feeding miracles to describe it, deliberately or not: took bread, gave thanks, broke it, began to eat. They were all encouraged and took some food themselves. In all, there were 276 of us on board. After the men had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea, Egypt's wheat to the fish, the cargo the whole voyage existed to deliver, jettisoned to buy the hull a few feet of draft.

When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they sighted a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. Cutting away the anchors, they left them in the sea as they loosened the ropes that held the rudders. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach. But the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was being broken up by the pounding of the waves. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none of them could swim to freedom, Rome's standing arithmetic for guards whose escaped prisoners cost them their own lives. But the centurion, wanting to spare Paul's life, thwarted their plan. He commanded those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. The rest were to follow on planks and various parts of the ship. In this way everyone was brought safely to land. Everyone: 276 swimmers and floaters, soldiers, sailors, prisoners, the prisoner-in-chief's company, on a beach none of them could name, in the rain that comes next. The angel's arithmetic balances to the man. Paul was right at Fair Havens and right in the storm, and the ship is firewood on a sandbar, and not a life is missing. What island this is, and what happens when the islanders meet the prisoner the sea delivered, closes the book.

title: Preaching the Kingdom, Unhindered
subtitle: Acts 28:1–31
description: Malta's kindness, a viper shaken off, and Rome at last: two whole years in a rented house, the kingdom preached boldly and freely.
paragraphs: Once we were safely ashore, we learned that the island was called Malta. The islanders showed us extraordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold. Paul gathered a bundle of sticks, and as he laid them on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself to his hand. When the islanders saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” But Paul shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no ill effects. The islanders were expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. But after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god. Malta runs the Lystra error in reverse order: first a murderer marked by heaven for death, then a god, and the man himself is neither, only a prisoner who shakes off a snake and goes back to gathering sticks. Luke records both verdicts of the crowd, as he recorded Lystra's, and lets Paul's silence be the correction.

Nearby stood an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days. The father of Publius was sick in bed, suffering from fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, and after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man. After this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well. The islanders honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail. Malta takes three months of winter off the voyage and pays for it in healings: the prisoner's last open-air ministry is an island clinic that began with a bonfire for shipwrecked strangers. After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island. It had the Twin Brothers as a figurehead, Castor and Pollux, the sailors' patron gods, carved on the bow of the ship that carries the apostle of the living God into Rome. Luke notes the figurehead the way he notes everything, without comment. Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days. From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium. After one day, a south wind came up, and on the second day we arrived at Puteoli.

There we found some brothers who invited us to spend the week with them. And so we came to Rome. The brothers there had heard about us and traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us, forty and thirty miles down the Appian Way, a welcoming party walking two days out of the city to meet a prisoner most of them had never seen, whose letter to their church they had been reading for years. When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God. When we arrived in Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him: house arrest in a rented home, one soldier, a chain, and the freedom to receive anyone. After three days, he called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans. They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me. But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, even though I have no charge to bring against my nation. So for this reason I have called to see you and speak with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” The leaders replied, “We have not received any letters about you from Judea, nor have any of the brothers from there reported or even mentioned anything bad about you. But we consider your views worth hearing, because we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.” Rome's synagogue leaders know nothing of the case and everything about the sect's reputation, and they book the prisoner a day.

So they set a day to meet with Paul, and many people came to the place he was staying. He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe. They disagreed among themselves and began to leave after Paul had made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: ‘Go to this people and say, “You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.” For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’ Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” It is the Pisidian Antioch sentence spoken for the last time, in the last room, at the end of the world the sentence described: the word to the Jew first, the refusal, the turn, and the listening Gentiles, performed now in the capital itself with the whole diaspora as its audience. Isaiah's hardening prophecy, quoted at every stage of this story since a voice in the temple gave it to a young prophet, is Paul's farewell to the synagogue he always entered first, and Luke closes the pattern the way he opened it, on Scripture.

Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ. And there the book ends. No trial before Caesar, no verdict, no release, no execution; Luke, who narrated two years of Caesarea custody in detail, stops his story at the threshold of the hearing the whole voyage aimed at, with the prisoner preaching in his own rented house to all comers. The last word of the Greek text is an adverb meaning unhindered, and the BSB's rendering catches it: freely. The chain is on his wrist and the word is unhindered in his mouth, in Rome, at the ends of the earth as the sentence of chapter 1 measured them, preached by the witness the Lord appointed on the Damascus road for exactly this. Whether Paul was released, retried, or executed under Nero belongs to the church's memory and to his own letters, and the epistles in this series will speak in their own slots. Luke's assignment was the road, and the road is finished: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth, one sentence of Jesus kept across twenty-eight chapters, ending not with a period but with a door standing open in a rented house in Rome.
